Architecture & Data Flow\n\n```\n   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n   │         Agent Harness (e.g., Pi Coding Agent)          │\n   │               with Qwen3.5-4B (Local)                  │\n   └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘\n                               │ MCP Request:\n                               │ get_adaptive_context(file, task_intent)\n                               ▼\n┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│                        ACC-MCP Server Engine                           │\n│                                                                        │\n│  1. AST Code Extractor                                                 │\n│     Parses target Python file into AST nodes, signatures, and deps.    │\n│                                                                        │\n│  2. Decision Model (Block 4)                                           │\n│     Extracts task & AST features -> computes P(Full Context Needed).   │\n│     Selects Tier 1, 2, or 3 based on decision threshold θ.             │\n│                                                                        │\n│  3. Hard Code Guardrail (Block 3)                                      │\n│     - Serves only .py files inside the workspace; secrets rejected.    │\n│     - Cuts output to a hard token ceiling (2,000 tokens).              │\n│                                                                        │\n│  4. Session Context Budget Tracker (Block 5)                           │\n│     Per-session token budget, ledger, and cached symbol index.         │\n└──────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘\n                               │ Return compressed AST slice\n                               ▼\n   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n   │             Qwen3.5-4B Generates Solution              │\n   │          (From a Compressed, Bounded Context)          │\n   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n---\n\n## 3. The 3-Tier Adaptive Compression Model\n\nWhen context is requested, the system compiles the code into one of three structural tiers:\n\n1. **Tier 1 (Signatures & Types):**  \n   Exports module structure, class definitions, function signatures, docstrings, and type hints. Omits all function bodies (`...`).\n2. **Tier 2 (Skeleton & Call-Graph Slice):**  \n   Exports Tier 1 plus direct callers (including callers in other workspace files), callees, and raised exceptions for the target symbol.\n3. **Tier 3 (Full Implementation Body):**  \n   Exports the source of the requested symbol verbatim from the file, with line numbers, cut to the 2,000-token ceiling.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Formalization & Mathematical Formulations\n\n### 4.1 Feature Extraction\nFor a given query $(T, F, S)$ where $T$ is the task intent string, $F$ is the target file, and $S$ is the target symbol:\n* $x_1 \\in \\{0, 1, 2\\}$: Task Intent Depth ($0 = \\text{inspect/call}$, $1 = \\text{refactor/patch interface}$, $2 = \\text{full algorithmic rewrite}$).\n* $x_2 \\in \\mathbb{N}$: Cyclomatic Complexity ($CC$) of symbol $S$.\n* $x_3 \\in \\mathbb{N}$: In-degree ($Deg_{in}$), the number of callers dependent on $S$.\n* $x_4 \\in \\{0, 1\\}$: Presence of explicit type hints and docstrings ($1$ if present, $0$ otherwise).\n\n### 4.2 Decision Model (Logistic Scoring Function)\nThe logit score $z$ determines the probability that the agent strictly requires the full implementation body (Tier 3):\n\n$$z = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + w_3 x_3 - w_4 x_4$$\n\nThe probability $P(\\text{Full Context Needed})$ is calculated as:\n\n$$P(\\text{Full}) = \\frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$$\n\n### 4.3 Decision Policy & Thresholds\nWith hand-picked thresholds $\\theta_{\\text{low}} = 0.30$ and $\\theta_{\\text{high}} = 0.65$ (the weights $w_0 \\dots w_4$ are fitted on training data, see Block 4):\n\n$$\\text{Tier}(P) = \\begin{cases} \n\\text{Tier 1 (Signatures Only)}, & \\text{if } P(\\text{Full}) < \\theta_{\\text{low}} \\\\\n\\text{Tier 2 (Skeleton Slice)}, & \\text{if } \\theta_{\\text{low}} \\le P(\\text{Full}) < \\theta_{\\text{high}} \\\\\n\\text{Tier 3 (Full Body)}, & \\text{if } P(\\text{Full}) \\ge \\theta_{\\text{high}}\n\\end{cases}$$\n\n### 4.4 Token Savings Metric\nFor each retrieval event, relative token reduction is computed against the raw full-file read:\n\n$$\\text{Savings (\\%)} = \\frac{\\text{Tokens}_{\\text{Full File}} - \\text{Tokens}_{\\text{Served Tier}}}{\\text{Tokens}_{\\text{Full File}}} \\times 100\\%$$\n\n---\n\n## 5. Mapping to the 5 Course Building Blocks\n\n### Block 2: Your Own MCP Server\n* **Implementation:** Built using the standard Python `mcp` SDK via stdio transport.\n* **Exposed Tools:**\n  * `get_adaptive_context(file_path: str, task_intent: str, symbol_name: str | None, min_tier: int | None)`: Runs the decision model and returns the slice; `min_tier` lets the agent ask for a higher tier when a slice was not enough.\n  * `find_symbol(name: str)`: Finds where a class, function, or method is defined in the workspace.\n  * `get_token_ledger()`: Returns token totals, `escalation_rate`, the session budget, and recent history.\n  * `reset_session()`: Starts a fresh session token budget for a new task.\n* **Evidence:** Tool tests in `tests/test_server.py`; a real agent session trace comes from the Pi runs in Phase 14.\n\n### Block 3: A Rule Enforced in Code\n* **Implementation:** A deterministic safety guardrail implemented in Python before any code is read or served.\n* **Enforced Rules:**\n  1. *Protected Path Rule:* Only `.py` files inside the workspace root are served, checked on the real path after symlinks; anything else (e.g. `.env`, `.git/`, `credentials.json`, `*.pem`, `../` traversal) raises `SecurityViolationError`.\n  2. *Hard Context Ceiling:* No slice is returned above $C_{\\max} = 2{,}000$ tokens (as counted by the server's token counter). Oversized slices are cut deterministically at statement boundaries, not by LLM prompting.\n* **Evidence:** `tests/test_guard.py` requests `.env`, paths outside the workspace, symlinks, and oversized files, and checks that they are rejected or cut in code.\n\n### Block 4: A Decision Model\n* **Implementation:** A logistic model whose weights are fitted by gradient descent on a train split; the thresholds are hand-picked.\n* **Evaluation:** 100 labeled task intents (29 Tier 1, 31 Tier 2, 40 Tier 3), split 70/30 by tier. Results are reported separately for train and for the 30-task holdout the fit never saw.\n* **Metrics:** 3x3 tier confusion matrix, false alarm rate (served a higher tier than needed), and miss rate (served a lower tier than needed). The holdout numbers are in `README.md`.\n\n### Block 5: Memory or Context Budget Management\n* **Implementation:** A per-session token budget plus a ledger that persists across server restarts.\n* **Mechanisms:**\n  * Caps the tokens served per session and steps down a tier when the chosen one does not fit.\n  * Persists the request history, totals, and the workspace symbol index to a local `context_budget.json` ledger.\n  * Restart test: after a restart the symbol index is rebuilt from the ledger and unchanged files are not parsed again (the file being served is still parsed for each request).\n\n### Block 9: A Measured Comparison\n* **Implementation:** Manual evaluation with the Pi coding agent on about 10 Python tasks from a public coding benchmark that come with tests (Phase 14 in `todo.md`).\n* **Comparison:**\n  * **Baseline:** Plain Pi with Qwen3.5-4B.\n  * **Gated:** Pi with Qwen3.5-4B and ACC-MCP.\n* **Reported Metrics:** Whether the task's tests pass, prompt tokens used, tiers served, and how often the agent escalated with `min_tier`.\n* **Where:** the protocol goes in `eval/PROTOCOL.md` and the results in `eval/results.md`. These runs have not been done yet.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Key Prompt Refinements & Architectural Evolutions\n\n### Refinement 1: Model-Agnostic Token Accounting Standard\n- **Initial Idea:** Hardcode token counting specifically for Qwen using a static tokenizer or fixed multiplier.\n- **Human Guidance:** *\"Does harness usually provide amount of spending tokens? Any existing standard? Why asking - yes, we are working with mainly one model - Qwen, but it will be better if we will be able to retrieve amount of tokens from the harness and/or from any model and not be tied to the only one selected.\"*\n- **Refined Engineering Solution:**\n  1. Implemented a pluggable pre-flight `TokenCounter` interface (`tokens.py`):\n     - `EndpointTokenCounter`: Queries local runner `/tokenize` endpoint (`llama-server` `POST /tokenize` or `Ollama` `POST /api/tokenize`).\n     - `HeuristicTokenCounter`: Fast offline fallback using `tiktoken` with character-ratio fallback.\n  2. Implemented post-flight ground-truth token accounting in the agent harness (`harness.py`), extracting `response[\"usage\"][\"prompt_tokens\"]` and reconciling it with `ContextBudgetTracker.reconcile_usage` in `src/acc_mcp/budget.py`. *(Both the harness and `reconcile_usage` were removed in Phase 13; the pluggable `TokenCounter` remains.)*\n\n### Refinement 2: Deterministic AST Node Slicing (No LLM Prompting)\n- **Initial Idea:** Use an LLM prompt to summarize oversized context when $C_{\\max}$ is exceeded.\n- **Requirement Rule (Block 3):** Under no circumstances can context exceed $C_{\\max} = 2,000$ tokens, and truncation must be enforced deterministically in code via AST node slicing, not by LLM prompting.\n- **Refined Engineering Solution:**\n  - Implemented `GuardRail.enforce_ceiling` in `guard.py` using AST statement-level slicing.\n  - Slices functions at statement boundaries, appending an `Ellipsis` (`...`) stub while preserving valid Python syntax.\n  - Slices classes by retaining class attributes and stubbing remaining methods.\n  - Identical input always produces identical output.\n  - *(Since Phase 15, Tier 3 is first cut by the parser on the original file text with an \"omitted lines\" note; `enforce_ceiling` remains as the final check.)*\n\n### Refinement 3: Action-Verb Intent Disambiguation\n- **Initial Observation:** Query `\"What is the parameter type for data?\"` was classified as Depth 1 because `\"parameter\"` was grouped under refactoring.\n- **Refinement:**\n  - Separated structural domain nouns (`parameter`, `interface`, `argument`, `type`) from active mutation verbs.\n  - Action verbs indicating inspection (`what is`, `check`, `show`, `view`, `inspect`) take precedence for Depth 0.\n  - Action verbs indicating interface mutation (`refactor`, `rename`, `patch`, `deprecate`, `trace callers`) define Depth 1.\n  - Action verbs indicating algorithmic overhaul (`rewrite`, `reimplement`, `fix bug`, `optimize`, `debug`) define Depth 2.\n  - Result at the time: 100% accuracy on the 20-task dataset. *(That dataset was used to tune the patterns and weights, so this was not a measurement on unseen data. On the Phase 21 holdout split the model gets 70%.)*\n\n### Refinement 4: Fitting the Decision Model and Choosing Thresholds (Phase 21)\n- **Task:** Replace the hand-picked weights with weights fitted on a train split, and report holdout numbers whatever they turn out to be.\n- **What the AI found:** The 20 original tasks gave $x_4 = 1$ for every task and $x_3 > 0$ only for Tier 2 tasks, so a fit would have learned \"has callers means Tier 2\" from a coincidence. The expanded dataset (100 tasks) puts called and unannotated symbols in every tier and phrases many intents without the classifier's keywords.\n- **Decision put to the human:** With the fitted weights, every $x_1 = 1$ intent lands at $P \\approx 0.55$–$0.72$, right on $\\theta_{\\text{high}} = 0.65$. The AI offered three options: keep 0.30/0.65 (holdout miss 14.3%, false alarm 33.3%), use the midpoints 0.25/0.75 (miss 38.1%, false alarm 5.6%), or also fit the thresholds.\n- **Human choice:** Keep 0.30/0.65 and fit only the weights, as the plan said (fewer misses, since too little context is worse than too much).\n- **Result:** Holdout accuracy 70.0% (hand-picked weights: 66.7%). Most errors come from the keyword classifier, not the weights.\n\n### Refinement 5: Documentation Must Match the Code (Phase 22)\n- **Task:** Remove README claims without evidence.\n- **Human choice:** The README named Qwen3.5-4B while the commands used Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. The human confirmed Qwen3.5-4B is the model actually used (already downloaded locally), and asked the AI not to download or run the model itself but to give commands instead.\n- **Removed or corrected claims:** tier token footprints (Tier 3 \"1,000–3,000 tokens\" contradicted the 2,000-token ceiling), \"more than 70% of queries need only interfaces\" and \"60–85% fewer prompt tokens\" (no measurement behind them), the Cerebras fallback (no code), `alembic/migrations/` as a protected path (no longer in `guard.py`), and `file:///Users/...` links (do not work on GitHub).\n\n---\n\n## 3. Manual Code Corrections & Debugging Annotations\n\n### Correction 1: Python 3.12 AST Unparse Quote Normalization\n- **Issue:** In `tests/test_guard.py` and `tests/test_harness.py`, assertions checked for double-quoted f-strings (e.g. `assert 'print(f\"Connecting to...\")' in output`). Python 3.12's `ast.unparse` formats single quotes by default (`print(f'Connecting to...')`), causing test failures.\n- **Correction:** Normalized assertions to substring checks and quote-agnostic pattern matching (`assert \"Connecting to\" in output`).\n\n### Correction 2: macOS `/var/folders` Temporary Path Handling\n- **Issue:** `GuardRail.validate_path` initially blocked all paths starting with `\"/var\"`. On macOS, `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` allocates paths under `/var/folders/...` (which maps to `/private/var/folders/`), causing temporary files in test runners to trigger `SecurityViolationError`.\n- **Correction:** Refined system root filtering in `guard.py`:\n  ```python\n  if norm_str.startswith((\"/etc\", \"/proc\", \"/sys\")):\n      return True\n  if norm_str.startswith(\"/var/\") and not norm_str.startswith((\"/var/folders\", \"/var/tmp\")):\n      return True\n  ```\n  *(Replaced in Phase 16 by the workspace-root rule: only `.py` files inside `ACC_MCP_ROOT` are served.)*\n\n### Correction 3: MCP 2.x SDK Migration (`FastMCP` $\\to$ `MCPServer`)\n- **Issue:** The official `mcp` SDK migrated from version 1.x to 2.x, renaming `FastMCP` to `MCPServer` in `mcp.server.mcpserver` and changing tool schema attributes (`input_schema` instead of `parameters`).\n- **Correction:** Added dual-import fallback in `src/acc_mcp/server.py` (and in the since-removed `harness.py`) supporting both MCP 1.x and 2.x, and updated tests to inspect `context_tool.input_schema`.\n\n### Correction 4: Tests That Silently Depended on the Hand-Picked Weights (Phase 21)\n- **Issue:** After the weights were fitted, the human ran the suite and reported one failure: `tests/test_callgraph.py::test_tier2_separates_resolved_and_possible_callers` (216 passed, 1 failed). The test checks the Tier 2 caller listing, but with the fitted weights \"Trace callers of Invoice.total\" gets $P \\approx 0.68 > 0.65$, so the server served Tier 3. The AI had pinned a similar test in `test_server.py` but missed this file.\n- **Correction:** Added a `policy_server_model` fixture in `tests/conftest.py` that builds the server with fixed weights, and used it in the three tests that check what a Tier 2 slice contains. Tests of the fit itself use the real defaults.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Exported session transcripts are in this folder (`*.md`).\n\n### Phases 1–10: First build\n\n| Phase | Core Objective | Key AI Contributions | Human Inquiries & Prompt Refinements |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| **Phase 1** | AST Parser & Tier 1 Compression | Implemented `ASTParser` and `Tier1Transformer` stubbing bodies with `...`. | Inquired about token standard; decoupled tokenizer into pluggable `TokenCounter`. |\n| **Phase 2** | Call-Graph & Complexity Metrics (Tier 2) | Built `CyclomaticComplexityVisitor` and `SymbolDependencyVisitor`. | Directed in-degree caller tracing and formatting of Tier 2 call-graph skeleton. |\n| **Phase 3** | Full Body & Guardrails (Block 3) | Implemented `Tier3Transformer`, `GuardRail.validate_path`, and AST ceiling. | Instructed deterministic statement-level AST slicing instead of LLM prompting. |\n| **Phase 4** | Decision Model (Block 4) | Built `TaskIntentClassifier`, feature fusion, and logistic scoring function. | Refined intent patterns to distinguish action verbs (inspect vs refactor vs rewrite). |\n| **Phase 5** | Decision Model Evaluation | Generated 20-task benchmark dataset, confusion matrix runner, and calibration. | Asked for zero critical misses and minimal false alarms. *(Later found to be measured on the same tasks used to pick the weights; replaced in Phase 21.)* |\n| **Phase 6** | Budget Tracker & Persistent Ledger (Block 5) | Built `ContextBudgetTracker`, JSON persistence, and symbol map cache. | Verified cold restart recovery preserving repository symbol maps without re-parsing. |\n| **Phase 7** | Stdio MCP Server Integration (Block 2) | Created stdio MCP server exposing `get_adaptive_context` and `get_token_ledger`. | Accommodated MCP 2.x migration (`MCPServer` vs `FastMCP`). |\n| **Phase 8** | Agent Harness & Model Integration (R1) | Developed OpenAI-compatible agent harness supporting local `llama-server` / `Ollama`. | Reconciled pre-flight estimates with ground-truth `usage.prompt_tokens`. *(Harness removed in Phase 13.)* |\n| **Phase 9** | Benchmark Suite (Block 9) | Created 30-run comparison runner `compare_context.py` and overflow failure trace. | Formulated oversized codebase to document baseline overflow crash vs gated success. *(Benchmark removed in Phase 13.)* |\n| **Phase 10** | Documentation & Verification (R1–R4) | Authored `README.md`, ran 110 automated tests, clean git state. | Final audit against all 5 building blocks and R1–R4 course requirements. *(Many claims later corrected in Phases 20–22.)* |\n\n### Phases 11–22: Review and rework\n\nAfter Phase 10 the project was reviewed and `todo.md` was extended with Phases 11–22 to fix what the review found (see `todo-generation-and-project-planning--8027412e.md`). For Phases 11–20 this log records only what `todo.md` and the commit history show; no separate notes on the prompts used in those sessions were kept.\n\n| Phase | Core Objective | What Was Done (from `todo.md` and commits) | Commit |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| **Phase 11** | Intent depth comes from the verb | Classifier counts operation verbs, not subject nouns like \"error\" or \"bug\". | `8b1e2b3` |\n| **Phase 12** | Tier escalation | Added `min_tier` to `get_adaptive_context` and tier guidance in the tool description. | `550c1b6` |\n| **Phase 13** | Remove synthetic benchmark | Deleted `compare_context.py`, `benchmark/`, and the in-process harness, because the benchmark marked every gated run as a success and one generated file produced most of its saving. | `f00e381` |\n| **Phase 14** | Pi integration & manual evaluation | **Not done yet.** Planned: workspace root setting, per-run ledger, Pi setup, `eval/PROTOCOL.md`, `eval/results.md`. (`ACC_MCP_ROOT` itself was added in Phase 16.) | — |\n| **Phase 15** | Edit-ready output | Tier 3 copied verbatim from the file, `# file lines a-b: symbol` headers, explicit \"omitted lines\" notes. | `be3b350` |\n| **Phase 16** | Path security | Only `.py` files inside the workspace root; resolved (symlink) paths checked. | `53bb6b4` |\n| **Phase 17** | Symbol index | Workspace index with SHA-256 hash-checked cache and the `find_symbol` tool. | `b5b36e2` |\n| **Phase 18** | Cross-file call graph | Callers found through imports; typed receivers resolved; unknown receivers listed as possible callers. | `96bde66` |\n| **Phase 19** | Session budget | Budget drives tier selection (step down, refuse forced tiers that do not fit), `reset_session`, one ledger save per request, history cap. | `17b713b` |\n| **Phase 20** | Decision model quick fixes | 3x3 confusion matrix, exact word-form keywords, `escalation_rate` in the ledger, README states the weights were hand-picked. | `048dcbf` |\n| **Phase 21** | Honest calibration | 100-task dataset, stratified 70/30 split, weights fitted by gradient descent, train and holdout reported separately. See Refinement 4. | `41b6c93` |\n| **Phase 22** | Documentation cleanup | README, `Description.md`, and this log aligned with the code; unsupported claims removed; `LICENSE` added. See Refinement 5. | pending |\n\n---\n\n## 2. Key Prompt Refinements & Architectural Evolutions\n\n### Refinement 1: Model-Agnostic Token Accounting Standard\n- **Initial Idea:** Hardcode token counting specifically for Qwen using a static tokenizer or fixed multiplier.\n- **Human Guidance:** *\"Does harness usually provide amount of spending tokens? Any existing standard? Why asking - yes, we are working with mainly one model - Qwen, but it will be better if we will be able to retrieve amount of tokens from the harness and/or from any model and not be tied to the only one selected.\"*\n- **Refined Engineering Solution:**\n  1. Implemented a pluggable pre-flight `TokenCounter` interface (`tokens.py`):\n     - `EndpointTokenCounter`: Queries local runner `/tokenize` endpoint (`llama-server` `POST /tokenize` or `Ollama` `POST /api/tokenize`).\n     - `HeuristicTokenCounter`: Fast offline fallback using `tiktoken` with character-ratio fallback.\n  2. Implemented post-flight ground-truth token accounting in the agent harness (`harness.py`), extracting `response[\"usage\"][\"prompt_tokens\"]` and reconciling it with `ContextBudgetTracker.reconcile_usage` in `src/acc_mcp/budget.py`. *(Both the harness and `reconcile_usage` were removed in Phase 13; the pluggable `TokenCounter` remains.)*\n\n### Refinement 2: Deterministic AST Node Slicing (No LLM Prompting)\n- **Initial Idea:** Use an LLM prompt to summarize oversized context when $C_{\\max}$ is exceeded.\n- **Requirement Rule (Block 3):** Under no circumstances can context exceed $C_{\\max} = 2,000$ tokens, and truncation must be enforced deterministically in code via AST node slicing, not by LLM prompting.\n- **Refined Engineering Solution:**\n  - Implemented `GuardRail.enforce_ceiling` in `guard.py` using AST statement-level slicing.\n  - Slices functions at statement boundaries, appending an `Ellipsis` (`...`) stub while preserving valid Python syntax.\n  - Slices classes by retaining class attributes and stubbing remaining methods.\n  - Identical input always produces identical output.\n  - *(Since Phase 15, Tier 3 is first cut by the parser on the original file text with an \"omitted lines\" note; `enforce_ceiling` remains as the final check.)*\n\n### Refinement 3: Action-Verb Intent Disambiguation\n- **Initial Observation:** Query `\"What is the parameter type for data?\"` was classified as Depth 1 because `\"parameter\"` was grouped under refactoring.\n- **Refinement:**\n  - Separated structural domain nouns (`parameter`, `interface`, `argument`, `type`) from active mutation verbs.\n  - Action verbs indicating inspection (`what is`, `check`, `show`, `view`, `inspect`) take precedence for Depth 0.\n  - Action verbs indicating interface mutation (`refactor`, `rename`, `patch`, `deprecate`, `trace callers`) define Depth 1.\n  - Action verbs indicating algorithmic overhaul (`rewrite`, `reimplement`, `fix bug`, `optimize`, `debug`) define Depth 2.\n  - Result at the time: 100% accuracy on the 20-task dataset. *(That dataset was used to tune the patterns and weights, so this was not a measurement on unseen data. On the Phase 21 holdout split the model gets 70%.)*\n\n### Refinement 4: Fitting the Decision Model and Choosing Thresholds (Phase 21)\n- **Task:** Replace the hand-picked weights with weights fitted on a train split, and report holdout numbers whatever they turn out to be.\n- **What the AI found:** The 20 original tasks gave $x_4 = 1$ for every task and $x_3 > 0$ only for Tier 2 tasks, so a fit would have learned \"has callers means Tier 2\" from a coincidence. The expanded dataset (100 tasks) puts called and unannotated symbols in every tier and phrases many intents without the classifier's keywords.\n- **Decision put to the human:** With the fitted weights, every $x_1 = 1$ intent lands at $P \\approx 0.55$–$0.72$, right on $\\theta_{\\text{high}} = 0.65$. The AI offered three options: keep 0.30/0.65 (holdout miss 14.3%, false alarm 33.3%), use the midpoints 0.25/0.75 (miss 38.1%, false alarm 5.6%), or also fit the thresholds.\n- **Human choice:** Keep 0.30/0.65 and fit only the weights, as the plan said (fewer misses, since too little context is worse than too much).\n- **Result:** Holdout accuracy 70.0% (hand-picked weights: 66.7%). Most errors come from the keyword classifier, not the weights.\n\n### Refinement 5: Documentation Must Match the Code (Phase 22)\n- **Task:** Remove README claims without evidence.\n- **Human choice:** The README named Qwen3.5-4B while the commands used Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. The human confirmed Qwen3.5-4B is the model actually used (already downloaded locally), and asked the AI not to download or run the model itself but to give commands instead.\n- **Removed or corrected claims:** tier token footprints (Tier 3 \"1,000–3,000 tokens\" contradicted the 2,000-token ceiling), \"more than 70% of queries need only interfaces\" and \"60–85% fewer prompt tokens\" (no measurement behind them), the Cerebras fallback (no code), `alembic/migrations/` as a protected path (no longer in `guard.py`), and `file:///Users/...` links (do not work on GitHub).\n\n---\n\n## 3. Manual Code Corrections & Debugging Annotations\n\n### Correction 1: Python 3.12 AST Unparse Quote Normalization\n- **Issue:** In `tests/test_guard.py` and `tests/test_harness.py`, assertions checked for double-quoted f-strings (e.g. `assert 'print(f\"Connecting to...\")' in output`). Python 3.12's `ast.unparse` formats single quotes by default (`print(f'Connecting to...')`), causing test failures.\n- **Correction:** Normalized assertions to substring checks and quote-agnostic pattern matching (`assert \"Connecting to\" in output`).\n\n### Correction 2: macOS `/var/folders` Temporary Path Handling\n- **Issue:** `GuardRail.validate_path` initially blocked all paths starting with `\"/var\"`. On macOS, `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` allocates paths under `/var/folders/...` (which maps to `/private/var/folders/`), causing temporary files in test runners to trigger `SecurityViolationError`.\n- **Correction:** Refined system root filtering in `guard.py`:\n  ```python\n  if norm_str.startswith((\"/etc\", \"/proc\", \"/sys\")):\n      return True\n  if norm_str.startswith(\"/var/\") and not norm_str.startswith((\"/var/folders\", \"/var/tmp\")):\n      return True\n  ```\n  *(Replaced in Phase 16 by the workspace-root rule: only `.py` files inside `ACC_MCP_ROOT` are served.)*\n\n### Correction 3: MCP 2.x SDK Migration (`FastMCP` $\\to$ `MCPServer`)\n- **Issue:** The official `mcp` SDK migrated from version 1.x to 2.x, renaming `FastMCP` to `MCPServer` in `mcp.server.mcpserver` and changing tool schema attributes (`input_schema` instead of `parameters`).\n- **Correction:** Added dual-import fallback in `src/acc_mcp/server.py` (and in the since-removed `harness.py`) supporting both MCP 1.x and 2.x, and updated tests to inspect `context_tool.input_schema`.\n\n### Correction 4: Tests That Silently Depended on the Hand-Picked Weights (Phase 21)\n- **Issue:** After the weights were fitted, the human ran the suite and reported one failure: `tests/test_callgraph.py::test_tier2_separates_resolved_and_possible_callers` (216 passed, 1 failed). The test checks the Tier 2 caller listing, but with the fitted weights \"Trace callers of Invoice.total\" gets $P \\approx 0.68 > 0.65$, so the server served Tier 3. The AI had pinned a similar test in `test_server.py` but missed this file.\n- **Correction:** Added a `policy_server_model` fixture in `tests/conftest.py` that builds the server with fixed weights, and used it in the three tests that check what a Tier 2 slice contains. Tests of the fit itself use the real defaults.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Verification Sign-Off\n\n### Phase 10 sign-off (superseded)\nThe Phase 10 sign-off reported 110 passing tests, \"full coverage\", and a 30-run comparative benchmark. {"parentUuid":"3e215cca-72d5-43e3-b609-99bfc2e550a4","isSidechain":false,"promptId":"1e96831a-174f-471b-b73e-b466fbdf8f4a","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_012PdXtzdcM1cSEiboWuaYKp","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# MCP Servers\n2\t\n3\tPi connects to [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) servers over stdio or streamable HTTP and makes their tools and resources available to the model.\n4\t\n5\t## Quick setup\n6\t\n7\tAdd a local stdio server, check the connection, then start Pi:\n8\t\n9\t```bash\n10\tpi mcp add filesystem -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem .\n11\tpi mcp list\n12\tpi\n13\t```\n14\t\n15\tFor a remote server:\n16\t\n17\t```bash\n18\tpi mcp add docs --url https://example.com/mcp --bearer-token-env-var DOCS_TOKEN\n19\tpi mcp list\n20\t```\n21\t\n22\tThese commands add user-level servers by default. Add `--local` or `-l` to write the project configuration instead:\n23\t\n24\t```bash\n25\tpi mcp add -l tools --env API_KEY='${TOOLS_KEY}' -- uvx tools-mcp\n26\t```\n27\t\n28\tUse `/mcp` inside an interactive session to inspect connections, sign in, reconnect, change exposure, or enable and disable servers. Run `/reload` after adding, removing, or changing a server outside the session.\n29\t\n30\t## Configure servers\n31\t\n32\tPi reads user-level servers from `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json` and project servers from `.pi/mcp.json`. Project configuration is read only after [project trust](security.md#understand-project-trust) is granted. A project entry replaces a user-level entry with the same name.\n33\t\n34\tA project entry without `command`, `url`, or `type` overrides only `enabled`, `exposure`, and `toolExposure` of the user-level server with the same name and keeps the rest, including `env`, `headers`, and `auth`. For example, this turns off a user-level server in one project:\n35\t\n36\t```json\n37\t{\n38\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n39\t    \"internal-tools\": { \"enabled\": false }\n40\t  }\n41\t}\n42\t```\n43\t\n44\tThe format matches other MCP clients:\n45\t\n46\t```json\n47\t{\n48\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n49\t    \"filesystem\": {\n50\t      \"command\": \"npx\",\n51\t      \"args\": [\"-y\", \"@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem\", \".\"]\n52\t    },\n53\t    \"docs\": {\n54\t      \"url\": \"https://example.com/mcp\",\n55\t      \"headers\": { \"Authorization\": \"Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}\" },\n56\t      \"description\": \"Search and read the product documentation\"\n57\t    }\n58\t  }\n59\t}\n60\t```\n61\t\n62\tStdio servers use `command`, `args`, `env`, and `cwd`. Relative `cwd` values resolve against the session directory. A leading `~/` in `command`, an argument, or `cwd` names the home directory.\n63\t\n64\tHTTP servers use `url`, `headers`, and `oauth` (see [Authenticate with OAuth](#authenticate-with-oauth)). The legacy SSE transport is not supported.\n65\t\n66\tBoth server types support:\n67\t\n68\t- `timeout`: per-request timeout in seconds (default 60). Progress notifications reset it.\n69\t- `enabled: false`: keep the entry without connecting to it.\n70\t- `exposure` and `toolExposure`: control how tools reach the model (see [Control tool exposure](#control-tool-exposure)).\n71\t- `description`: what the server offers, in a sentence. It lists the server in the system prompt (see [Control tool exposure](#control-tool-exposure)), tool search ranks the server's tools by it, and codemode's `describeNamespace()` returns it. Without it, the first line of the server instructions is used once the server connects.\n72\t\n73\tKeep personal servers and servers with credentials in the user-level file. Use the project file only for servers the project requires, and only in trusted projects.\n74\t\n75\t### Configuration rules\n76\t\n77\t- Server names may contain only letters, digits, `_`, and `-`. Tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, with every character other than letters, digits, and `_` replaced by `_`; tools of a server whose names then collide all get a hash suffix. Server names that differ only in `-` and `_` count as the same server: a second one is rejected, and a `mcp.json` server overrides a registered one.\n78\t- `type` is optional. A `command` selects stdio and a `url` selects streamable HTTP. When present, `type` must be `stdio`, `http`, or `streamable-http`.\n79\t- `sse` is rejected. Servers that document an SSE endpoint often also provide streamable HTTP, commonly at `/mcp` instead of `/sse`.\n80\t- `command` is one executable and `args` contains its arguments. It is not a shell command string.\n81\t- `env` and `headers` values can use environment variables such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. They can also run a command with `!command`, but the command must make up the whole value, for example `\"Authorization\": \"!echo Bearer $(gh auth token)\"`.\n82\t- Invalid entries are reported and skipped without preventing other servers from connecting.\n83\t\n84\t`pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` cover common changes from a shell. See [MCP commands](cli.md#mcp-commands) for their options.\n85\t\n86\t### Inspect or change a server\n87\t\n88\t`/mcp` lists configured servers with their state, tool count, exposure, and configuration source. Servers that need attention appear first. Select a server to inspect its tools and connection details, reconnect, sign in or out, change exposure, or enable and disable it.\n89\t\n90\tExposure and enabled-state changes are saved to the file that defines the server without replacing unrelated content. In a trusted project, \"Enable in this project\" and \"Disable in this project\" add a project override for a user-level server; later changes to that server are saved to the override. Disabled servers remain listed. Outside the interactive TUI, `/mcp` prints server status; `/mcp login <server>`, `/mcp logout <server>`, and `/mcp reconnect <server>` perform those actions directly.\n91\t\n92\tShell commands work without a session: `pi mcp add`, `pi mcp remove`, `pi mcp list`, `pi mcp login`, and `pi mcp logout`. Shell commands do not load extensions.\n93\t\n94\t### Diagnose connection problems\n95\t\n96\tRun `pi mcp list` to connect to every enabled server and print its state, tools, and errors. It exits with status 1 when an entry is invalid or an enabled server is not connected. `/mcp` shows the full connection error and the tail of stderr from a failed stdio server.\n97\t\n98\tPi reports configuration errors, failed connections, and required sign-ins once after startup. Server logging notifications are appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log` as `<time> [<server>] <level> <logger>: <message>`. The file moves to `mcp.log.1` after it grows past 5 MB.\n99\t\n100\tPi connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts. A server's tools appear once it connects; the `codemode` description does not list them, so it does not change when servers connect. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools, which must be declared in its request. Other servers are waited for when they are needed: a codemode script waits for the servers it names (`mcp__<server>`) and, when it calls `searchTools()` or reads `ALL_TOOLS`, for all of them; `tool_search` and the resource tools also wait for all of them. HTTP network errors and transient statuses (408, 429, and 5xx) are retried twice. A dropped connection is shown as disconnected and reconnects on the next call. When a server announces a changed tool list, new tools are added and withdrawn tools become unreachable.\n101\t\n102\tStopping a stdio server closes its stdin, sends SIGTERM, then sends SIGKILL to its process group. This also stops servers launched through wrappers such as `npx` or `uvx`.\n103\t\n104\t## Migrate configuration from another client\n105\t\n106\tMove the converted entry under `mcpServers` in `mcp.json`, then run `pi mcp list` to validate it.\n107\t\n108\t| Client | Conversion |\n109\t|---|---|\n110\t| Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or Cursor | Copy the existing `mcpServers` entry. |\n111\t| VS Code | Move an entry from the top-level `servers` object and replace `${input:...}` prompts with `${NAME}` environment variables. |\n112\t| Codex | Convert `[mcp_servers.<name>]` TOML fields such as `command`, `args`, `env`, and `url` to JSON. |\n113\t| OpenCode | Convert `\"type\": \"local\"` to a stdio entry, split its `command` array into `command` and `args`, rename `environment` to `env`, and replace `{env:NAME}` with `${NAME}`. Convert `\"type\": \"remote\"` to a URL entry. |\n114\t\n115\t## Authenticate with OAuth\n116\t\n117\tRemote servers that use OAuth, such as Sentry, need no credentials in `mcp.json`:\n118\t\n119\t```json\n120\t{\n121\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n122\t    \"sentry\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp\" }\n123\t  }\n124\t}\n125\t```\n126\t\n127\tWhen the server rejects an unauthenticated connection, `/mcp` shows that it needs sign-in. Select \"Sign in\", run `/mcp login sentry`, or run `pi mcp login sentry`. Pi opens the authorization page and waits for approval. If the browser runs on another machine, such as over SSH, paste its redirected URL into the sign-in screen. A running session uses the new credentials on its next turn.\n128\t\n129\tPi registers itself with the authorization server, stores tokens in `~/.pi/agent/mcp-auth.json`, and refreshes access tokens when they expire or the server rejects them. If a server later requests additional scope, Pi asks for sign-in again. Signing out deletes the stored credentials.\n130\t\n131\tCredentials belong to a server name and URL. Servers with the same URL under different names, such as one per account, sign in separately; servers with the same name and URL in different `mcp.json` files share one sign-in.\n132\t\n133\tOAuth applies to HTTP servers without an `Authorization` header. For a server that does not support dynamic client registration, configure a registered client:\n134\t\n135\t```json\n136\t{\n137\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n138\t    \"example\": {\n139\t      \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\",\n140\t      \"oauth\": { \"clientId\": \"my-client\", \"clientSecret\": \"${EXAMPLE_SECRET}\", \"callbackPort\": 8765 }\n141\t    }\n142\t  }\n143\t}\n144\t```\n145\t\n146\tThe redirect URI must match the registered URI. `callbackPort` uses `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. To use another URI, set `callbackUrl`; it must use HTTP on `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`. Pi sends it exactly as written. When `callbackUrl` omits a port, Pi uses `callbackPort` or a free port and adds it to the URI, as allowed for loopback redirects by RFC 8252. `clientSecret` is optional and can use an environment variable or command.\n147\t\n148\tSet `scope` to a space-separated list for servers that do not advertise their required scopes. Otherwise, Pi requests the advertised scopes. Later scope requests are added to the configured value.\n149\t\n150\tPi registers as `pi`. Some servers only accept registrations from known clients. Set `clientName` to send another name:\n151\t\n152\t```json\n153\t{\n154\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n155\t    \"figma\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.figma.com/mcp\", \"oauth\": { \"clientName\": \"Claude Code\" } }\n156\t  }\n157\t}\n158\t```\n159\t\n160\tThe name is only sent when Pi registers a client. To register again under a new name, sign out first.\n161\t\n162\tSome authorization servers allow clients by their Client ID Metadata Document URL instead of registering them. Set `clientRegistration` to `cimd` to identify as Pi's document on pi.dev instead of registering:\n163\t\n164\t```json\n165\t{\n166\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n167\t    \"example\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\", \"oauth\": { \"clientRegistration\": \"cimd\" } }\n168\t  }\n169\t}\n170\t```\n171\t\n172\tThe client ID is `https://pi.dev/oauth/client.json` with the redirect URI `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. If the authorization server does not send the `iss` parameter in authorization responses (RFC 9207), Pi uses a document and redirect path specific to the MCP server instead: `https://pi.dev/oauth/<id>/client.json` with `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback/<id>`. The authorization server must advertise Client ID Metadata Document support and public clients, or sign-in fails. `cimd` cannot be combined with `clientId` or `clientName`, and a `callbackUrl` must use `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` with the path `/callback`.\n173\t\n174\tPi finds the authorization server through the server's protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) and checks that the authorization server's metadata names the expected issuer (RFC 8414). Some servers advertise the wrong authorization server or none, so sign-in opens a page that does not exist. Set `authServerMetadataUrl` to the metadata document of the right authorization server:\n175\t\n176\t```json\n177\t{\n178\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n179\t    \"example\": {\n180\t      \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\",\n181\t      \"oauth\": { \"authServerMetadataUrl\": \"https://example.okta.com/.well-known/openid-configuration\" }\n182\t    }\n183\t  }\n184\t}\n185\t```\n186\t\n187\tPi uses that document instead of discovery and trusts it as configured, so only point it at a document you trust. The URL must use HTTPS, except on `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`.\n188\t\n189\t## Control tool exposure\n190\t\n191\tEach server tool is registered as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. The server's `exposure` determines how the model reaches it:\n192\t\n193\t| Exposure | Behavior | Typical use |\n194\t|---|---|---|\n195\t| `codemode` (default) | Callable from [`codemode`](cli.md#tools) scripts, but neither declared to the model nor listed in the codemode description. Scripts find tools with `searchTools()`, `describeTool()`, or `ALL_TOOLS`. | General MCP servers, especially when scripts should combine or filter calls. |\n196\t| `deferred` | Not declared until [`tool_search`](cli.md#tools) loads a match for the next model call. | Large servers whose tools should be called directly after discovery. |\n197\t| `direct` | Declared to the model like a built-in tool and also callable from codemode. | Small, frequently used tool sets. |\n198\t| `hidden` | Registered but unreachable. | Servers or tools that should remain unavailable. |\n199\t\n200\t`codemode-deferred` is accepted as an alias for `codemode`.\n201\t\n202\tServers with `codemode` or `deferred` tools are listed in the `mcp_servers` section of the system prompt, with how their tools are reached and one line from the configured `description` or, once connected, from the server instructions. Pi updates the section when a prompt starts, after waiting for servers with `direct` tools. When it changed, for example because a server connected and its summary became available, Pi appends the new section to the conversation instead of changing tool declarations, so earlier messages stay cached. `describeNamespace()` and the `namespace` option of `searchTools()` accept `mcp__dev-radius`, `mcp__dev_radius`, `dev-radius`, or `dev_radius`.\n203\t\n204\tPi activates `codemode` when a server with `codemode` exposure connects. It activates `tool_search` for a server with `deferred` exposure. To make the model see a tool without searching, give it `direct` exposure with `toolExposure`.\n205\t\n206\t`toolExposure` overrides the server exposure for individual tools. Keys are exact server tool names or patterns where `*` matches any characters. Exact names win over patterns; among patterns, the first match wins. A server with `hidden` exposure can expose only selected tools:\n207\t\n208\t```json\n209\t{\n210\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n211\t    \"github\": {\n212\t      \"url\": \"https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/\",\n213\t      \"exposure\": \"deferred\",\n214\t      \"toolExposure\": {\n215\t        \"search_code\": \"direct\",\n216\t        \"get_*\": \"codemode\",\n217\t        \"delete_*\": \"hidden\"\n218\t      }\n219\t    }\n220\t  }\n221\t}\n222\t```\n223\t\n224\t`pi mcp list` marks tools whose exposure differs from their server. The Tools view in `/mcp` also shows the effective exposure.\n225\t\n226\tTools with `codemode` or `deferred` exposure can be reached through either indirect mechanism: codemode scripts can call them, and `tool_search` can load them. Codemode calls do not depend on the active tool set, so they remain available after `/tree`, resume, and fork. Tools loaded by `tool_search` are recorded in the transcript and remain declared on that branch.\n227\t\n228\tTo keep `codemode` active without MCP servers, add `\"defaultTools\": [\"+codemode\"]` to [settings](settings.md#tools). To prevent automatic codemode activation, set `\"autoEnableCodemode\": false` beside `mcpServers`. A project value overrides the user-level value. Pi warns once when neither `codemode` nor `tool_search` is active and non-direct tools cannot be called.\n229\t\n230\tText results over 20 KB reach the model with their middle removed around a `…N chars truncated…` marker. The full text is saved to a temporary file named in the result. Codemode scripts receive the complete result and can reduce it before returning output to the model.\n231\t\n232\tCodemode scripts receive the complete MCP `CallToolResult`, including `content`, `structuredContent`, and `isError`. A result with `isError` resolves inside scripts but is reported as an error for direct calls. `image(result.content[0])` forwards an image block. Server instructions are not part of any tool description; scripts read them with `describeNamespace(\"mcp__<server>\")`, which also returns the server's tool names.\n233\t\n234\t## Use resources\n235\t\n236\tWhen a connected server offers [resources](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/resources), Pi adds the resource tools used by Codex and OpenCode:\n237\t\n238\t- `list_mcp_resources` lists resources as JSON: `{ server?, resources: [{ server, uri, name, ... }], nextCursor? }`. With `server`, it lists one page; `cursor` continues with the next page. Without `server`, it lists every resource from every server.\n239\t- `list_mcp_resource_templates` lists URI templates for resources the servers do not list directly.\n240\t- `read_mcp_resource` reads a resource by `server` and `uri`. Text reaches the model as text and images as images. Other binary resources are saved to temporary files, and the model receives the path. Scripts receive `{ server, uri, contents }`.\n241\t\n242\tThese tools reach every enabled, non-hidden server with resources. Their exposure is the widest exposure among those servers: `direct`, then `codemode` or `deferred`. Resource links in tool results identify `read_mcp_resource` and the server.\n243\t\n244\tResources for MCP Apps, identified by `ui://` URIs or `text/html;profile=mcp-app`, are omitted because Pi does not render them. Resource icons are also omitted.\n245\t\n246\tReading and listing resources is retried once after a transient HTTP error (408, 429, or 5xx). Tool calls are not retried because the server may already have performed them.\n247\t\n248\t## Permissions\n249\t\n250\tEvery MCP call passes through Pi's tool pipeline. Extension `tool_call` and `tool_result` handlers, including permission gates, therefore apply to MCP tools. Calls made from codemode scripts carry the codemode call ID as `parentToolCallId`.\n251\t\n252\t`pi.getAllTools()` reports the annotations declared by each server: `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, and `openWorldHint`. Permission extensions can use these hints to decide which calls require confirmation (see [Tool exposure](extensions.md#tool-exposure)). Add `--local` or `-l` to write the project configuration instead:\n\n```bash\npi mcp add -l tools --env API_KEY='${TOOLS_KEY}' -- uvx tools-mcp\n```\n\nUse `/mcp` inside an interactive session to inspect connections, sign in, reconnect, change exposure, or enable and disable servers. Run `/reload` after adding, removing, or changing a server outside the session.\n\n## Configure servers\n\nPi reads user-level servers from `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json` and project servers from `.pi/mcp.json`. Project configuration is read only after [project trust](security.md#understand-project-trust) is granted. A project entry replaces a user-level entry with the same name.\n\nA project entry without `command`, `url`, or `type` overrides only `enabled`, `exposure`, and `toolExposure` of the user-level server with the same name and keeps the rest, including `env`, `headers`, and `auth`. For example, this turns off a user-level server in one project:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"internal-tools\": { \"enabled\": false }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe format matches other MCP clients:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"filesystem\": {\n      \"command\": \"npx\",\n      \"args\": [\"-y\", \"@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem\", \".\"]\n    },\n    \"docs\": {\n      \"url\": \"https://example.com/mcp\",\n      \"headers\": { \"Authorization\": \"Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}\" },\n      \"description\": \"Search and read the product documentation\"\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nStdio servers use `command`, `args`, `env`, and `cwd`. Relative `cwd` values resolve against the session directory. A leading `~/` in `command`, an argument, or `cwd` names the home directory.\n\nHTTP servers use `url`, `headers`, and `oauth` (see [Authenticate with OAuth](#authenticate-with-oauth)). The legacy SSE transport is not supported.\n\nBoth server types support:\n\n- `timeout`: per-request timeout in seconds (default 60). Progress notifications reset it.\n- `enabled: false`: keep the entry without connecting to it.\n- `exposure` and `toolExposure`: control how tools reach the model (see [Control tool exposure](#control-tool-exposure)).\n- `description`: what the server offers, in a sentence. It lists the server in the system prompt (see [Control tool exposure](#control-tool-exposure)), tool search ranks the server's tools by it, and codemode's `describeNamespace()` returns it. Without it, the first line of the server instructions is used once the server connects.\n\nKeep personal servers and servers with credentials in the user-level file. Use the project file only for servers the project requires, and only in trusted projects.\n\n### Configuration rules\n\n- Server names may contain only letters, digits, `_`, and `-`. Tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, with every character other than letters, digits, and `_` replaced by `_`; tools of a server whose names then collide all get a hash suffix. Server names that differ only in `-` and `_` count as the same server: a second one is rejected, and a `mcp.json` server overrides a registered one.\n- `type` is optional. A `command` selects stdio and a `url` selects streamable HTTP. When present, `type` must be `stdio`, `http`, or `streamable-http`.\n- `sse` is rejected. Servers that document an SSE endpoint often also provide streamable HTTP, commonly at `/mcp` instead of `/sse`.\n- `command` is one executable and `args` contains its arguments. It is not a shell command string.\n- `env` and `headers` values can use environment variables such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. They can also run a command with `!command`, but the command must make up the whole value, for example `\"Authorization\": \"!echo Bearer $(gh auth token)\"`.\n- Invalid entries are reported and skipped without preventing other servers from connecting.\n\n`pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` cover common changes from a shell. See [MCP commands](cli.md#mcp-commands) for their options.\n\n### Inspect or change a server\n\n`/mcp` lists configured servers with their state, tool count, exposure, and configuration source. Servers that need attention appear first. Select a server to inspect its tools and connection details, reconnect, sign in or out, change exposure, or enable and disable it.\n\nExposure and enabled-state changes are saved to the file that defines the server without replacing unrelated content. In a trusted project, \"Enable in this project\" and \"Disable in this project\" add a project override for a user-level server; later changes to that server are saved to the override. Disabled servers remain listed. Outside the interactive TUI, `/mcp` prints server status; `/mcp login <server>`, `/mcp logout <server>`, and `/mcp reconnect <server>` perform those actions directly.\n\nShell commands work without a session: `pi mcp add`, `pi mcp remove`, `pi mcp list`, `pi mcp login`, and `pi mcp logout`. Shell commands do not load extensions.\n\n### Diagnose connection problems\n\nRun `pi mcp list` to connect to every enabled server and print its state, tools, and errors. It exits with status 1 when an entry is invalid or an enabled server is not connected. `/mcp` shows the full connection error and the tail of stderr from a failed stdio server.\n\nPi reports configuration errors, failed connections, and required sign-ins once after startup. Server logging notifications are appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log` as `<time> [<server>] <level> <logger>: <message>`. The file moves to `mcp.log.1` after it grows past 5 MB.\n\nPi connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts. A server's tools appear once it connects; the `codemode` description does not list them, so it does not change when servers connect. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools, which must be declared in its request. Other servers are waited for when they are needed: a codemode script waits for the servers it names (`mcp__<server>`) and, when it calls `searchTools()` or reads `ALL_TOOLS`, for all of them; `tool_search` and the resource tools also wait for all of them. HTTP network errors and transient statuses (408, 429, and 5xx) are retried twice. A dropped connection is shown as disconnected and reconnects on the next call. When a server announces a changed tool list, new tools are added and withdrawn tools become unreachable.\n\nStopping a stdio server closes its stdin, sends SIGTERM, then sends SIGKILL to its process group. This also stops servers launched through wrappers such as `npx` or `uvx`.\n\n## Migrate configuration from another client\n\nMove the converted entry under `mcpServers` in `mcp.json`, then run `pi mcp list` to validate it.\n\n| Client | Conversion |\n|---|---|\n| Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or Cursor | Copy the existing `mcpServers` entry. |\n| VS Code | Move an entry from the top-level `servers` object and replace `${input:...}` prompts with `${NAME}` environment variables. |\n| Codex | Convert `[mcp_servers.<name>]` TOML fields such as `command`, `args`, `env`, and `url` to JSON. |\n| OpenCode | Convert `\"type\": \"local\"` to a stdio entry, split its `command` array into `command` and `args`, rename `environment` to `env`, and replace `{env:NAME}` with `${NAME}`. Convert `\"type\": \"remote\"` to a URL entry. |\n\n## Authenticate with OAuth\n\nRemote servers that use OAuth, such as Sentry, need no credentials in `mcp.json`:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"sentry\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp\" }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nWhen the server rejects an unauthenticated connection, `/mcp` shows that it needs sign-in. Select \"Sign in\", run `/mcp login sentry`, or run `pi mcp login sentry`. Pi opens the authorization page and waits for approval. If the browser runs on another machine, such as over SSH, paste its redirected URL into the sign-in screen. A running session uses the new credentials on its next turn.\n\nPi registers itself with the authorization server, stores tokens in `~/.pi/agent/mcp-auth.json`, and refreshes access tokens when they expire or the server rejects them. If a server later requests additional scope, Pi asks for sign-in again. Signing out deletes the stored credentials.\n\nCredentials belong to a server name and URL. Servers with the same URL under different names, such as one per account, sign in separately; servers with the same name and URL in different `mcp.json` files share one sign-in.\n\nOAuth applies to HTTP servers without an `Authorization` header. For a server that does not support dynamic client registration, configure a registered client:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"example\": {\n      \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\",\n      \"oauth\": { \"clientId\": \"my-client\", \"clientSecret\": \"${EXAMPLE_SECRET}\", \"callbackPort\": 8765 }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe redirect URI must match the registered URI. `callbackPort` uses `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. To use another URI, set `callbackUrl`; it must use HTTP on `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`. Pi sends it exactly as written. When `callbackUrl` omits a port, Pi uses `callbackPort` or a free port and adds it to the URI, as allowed for loopback redirects by RFC 8252. `clientSecret` is optional and can use an environment variable or command.\n\nSet `scope` to a space-separated list for servers that do not advertise their required scopes. Otherwise, Pi requests the advertised scopes. Later scope requests are added to the configured value.\n\nPi registers as `pi`. Some servers only accept registrations from known clients. Set `clientName` to send another name:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"figma\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.figma.com/mcp\", \"oauth\": { \"clientName\": \"Claude Code\" } }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe name is only sent when Pi registers a client. To register again under a new name, sign out first.\n\nSome authorization servers allow clients by their Client ID Metadata Document URL instead of registering them. Set `clientRegistration` to `cimd` to identify as Pi's document on pi.dev instead of registering:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"example\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\", \"oauth\": { \"clientRegistration\": \"cimd\" } }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe client ID is `https://pi.dev/oauth/client.json` with the redirect URI `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. If the authorization server does not send the `iss` parameter in authorization responses (RFC 9207), Pi uses a document and redirect path specific to the MCP server instead: `https://pi.dev/oauth/<id>/client.json` with `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback/<id>`. The authorization server must advertise Client ID Metadata Document support and public clients, or sign-in fails. `cimd` cannot be combined with `clientId` or `clientName`, and a `callbackUrl` must use `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` with the path `/callback`.\n\nPi finds the authorization server through the server's protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) and checks that the authorization server's metadata names the expected issuer (RFC 8414). Some servers advertise the wrong authorization server or none, so sign-in opens a page that does not exist. Set `authServerMetadataUrl` to the metadata document of the right authorization server:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"example\": {\n      \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\",\n      \"oauth\": { \"authServerMetadataUrl\": \"https://example.okta.com/.well-known/openid-configuration\" }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nPi uses that document instead of discovery and trusts it as configured, so only point it at a document you trust. The URL must use HTTPS, except on `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`.\n\n## Control tool exposure\n\nEach server tool is registered as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. The server's `exposure` determines how the model reaches it:\n\n| Exposure | Behavior | Typical use |\n|---|---|---|\n| `codemode` (default) | Callable from [`codemode`](cli.md#tools) scripts, but neither declared to the model nor listed in the codemode description. Scripts find tools with `searchTools()`, `describeTool()`, or `ALL_TOOLS`. | General MCP servers, especially when scripts should combine or filter calls. |\n| `deferred` | Not declared until [`tool_search`](cli.md#tools) loads a match for the next model call. | Large servers whose tools should be called directly after discovery. |\n| `direct` | Declared to the model like a built-in tool and also callable from codemode. | Small, frequently used tool sets. |\n| `hidden` | Registered but unreachable. | Servers or tools that should remain unavailable. |\n\n`codemode-deferred` is accepted as an alias for `codemode`.\n\nServers with `codemode` or `deferred` tools are listed in the `mcp_servers` section of the system prompt, with how their tools are reached and one line from the configured `description` or, once connected, from the server instructions. Pi updates the section when a prompt starts, after waiting for servers with `direct` tools. When it changed, for example because a server connected and its summary became available, Pi appends the new section to the conversation instead of changing tool declarations, so earlier messages stay cached. `describeNamespace()` and the `namespace` option of `searchTools()` accept `mcp__dev-radius`, `mcp__dev_radius`, `dev-radius`, or `dev_radius`.\n\nPi activates `codemode` when a server with `codemode` exposure connects. It activates `tool_search` for a server with `deferred` exposure. To make the model see a tool without searching, give it `direct` exposure with `toolExposure`.\n\n`toolExposure` overrides the server exposure for individual tools. Keys are exact server tool names or patterns where `*` matches any characters. Exact names win over patterns; among patterns, the first match wins. A server with `hidden` exposure can expose only selected tools:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"github\": {\n      \"url\": \"https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/\",\n      \"exposure\": \"deferred\",\n      \"toolExposure\": {\n        \"search_code\": \"direct\",\n        \"get_*\": \"codemode\",\n        \"delete_*\": \"hidden\"\n      }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\n`pi mcp list` marks tools whose exposure differs from their server. The Tools view in `/mcp` also shows the effective exposure.\n\nTools with `codemode` or `deferred` exposure can be reached through either indirect mechanism: codemode scripts can call them, and `tool_search` can load them. Codemode calls do not depend on the active tool set, so they remain available after `/tree`, resume, and fork. Tools loaded by `tool_search` are recorded in the transcript and remain declared on that branch.\n\nTo keep `codemode` active without MCP servers, add `\"defaultTools\": [\"+codemode\"]` to [settings](settings.md#tools). To prevent automatic codemode activation, set `\"autoEnableCodemode\": false` beside `mcpServers`. A project value overrides the user-level value. Pi warns once when neither `codemode` nor `tool_search` is active and non-direct tools cannot be called.\n\nText results over 20 KB reach the model with their middle removed around a `…N chars truncated…` marker. The full text is saved to a temporary file named in the result. Codemode scripts receive the complete result and can reduce it before returning output to the model.\n\nCodemode scripts receive the complete MCP `CallToolResult`, including `content`, `structuredContent`, and `isError`. A result with `isError` resolves inside scripts but is reported as an error for direct calls. `image(result.content[0])` forwards an image block. Server instructions are not part of any tool description; scripts read them with `describeNamespace(\"mcp__<server>\")`, which also returns the server's tool names.\n\n## Use resources\n\nWhen a connected server offers [resources](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/resources), Pi adds the resource tools used by Codex and OpenCode:\n\n- `list_mcp_resources` lists resources as JSON: `{ server?, resources: [{ server, uri, name, ... }], nextCursor? }`. With `server`, it lists one page; `cursor` continues with the next page. Without `server`, it lists every resource from every server.\n- `list_mcp_resource_templates` lists URI templates for resources the servers do not list directly.\n- `read_mcp_resource` reads a resource by `server` and `uri`. Text reaches the model as text and images as images. Other binary resources are saved to temporary files, and the model receives the path. Scripts receive `{ server, uri, contents }`.\n\nThese tools reach every enabled, non-hidden server with resources. Their exposure is the widest exposure among those servers: `direct`, then `codemode` or `deferred`. Resource links in tool results identify `read_mcp_resource` and the server.\n\nResources for MCP Apps, identified by `ui://` URIs or `text/html;profile=mcp-app`, are omitted because Pi does not render them. Resource icons are also omitted.\n\nReading and listing resources is retried once after a transient HTTP error (408, 429, or 5xx). Tool calls are not retried because the server may already have performed them.\n\n## Permissions\n\nEvery MCP call passes through Pi's tool pipeline. Extension `tool_call` and `tool_result` handlers, including permission gates, therefore apply to MCP tools. Calls made from codemode scripts carry the codemode call ID as `parentToolCallId`.\n\n`pi.getAllTools()` reports the annotations declared by each server: `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, and `openWorldHint`. Permission extensions can use these hints to decide which calls require confirmation (see [Tool exposure](extensions.md#tool-exposure)). Resource tools are marked read-only.\n\n## Extensions and SDK\n\n### Add servers from extensions\n\nExtensions can add servers for the current session with `pi.registerMcpServer(name, config)`, using the same shape as an `mcpServers` entry (see [MCP servers in extensions](extensions.md#mcp-servers)). Registered servers connect like configured servers and appear in `/mcp` with the extension as their source.\n\nChanges to enabled state or exposure apply only to the current session. A file-configured server with the same name takes precedence, and `/mcp` lists the overridden registration. `pi mcp` shell commands do not load extensions and only see file-configured servers.\n\n### Replace the built-in MCP support\n\nAn installed extension that registers `/mcp`, such as `pi-mcp-adapter`, replaces the built-in MCP support for sessions. Pi then does not read `mcp.json` or connect its servers in a session, and `/mcp` belongs to the extension. Remove the extension to restore the built-in behavior. Shell-level `pi mcp` commands always use the built-in implementation.\n\n### Use MCP from the SDK\n\nSDK sessions do not load built-in extensions. Add the MCP extension, the codemode extension for `codemode` servers, and the tool-search extension for `deferred` servers to the resource loader. Labels are letters for a choice (up to 62 options), `Yes`/`No` for a bool, and digits for a score (up to 10 levels). The second copy of the state is read with the questions in view, which improved accuracy on JevBench with small models. Pi reads the probabilities of the labels as the next token and normalizes them. A choice returns every option's probability and a confidence of `(n * peak - 1) / (n - 1)`; a score returns the expected level.\n94\t\n95\t- Raw label probabilities are usually overconfident.
