Add `--local` or `-l` to write the project configuration instead:\n23\t\n24\t```bash\n25\tpi mcp add -l tools --env API_KEY='${TOOLS_KEY}' -- uvx tools-mcp\n26\t```\n27\t\n28\tUse `/mcp` inside an interactive session to inspect connections, sign in, reconnect, change exposure, or enable and disable servers. Run `/reload` after adding, removing, or changing a server outside the session.\n29\t\n30\t## Configure servers\n31\t\n32\tPi reads user-level servers from `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json` and project servers from `.pi/mcp.json`. Project configuration is read only after [project trust](security.md#understand-project-trust) is granted. A project entry replaces a user-level entry with the same name.\n33\t\n34\tA project entry without `command`, `url`, or `type` overrides only `enabled`, `exposure`, and `toolExposure` of the user-level server with the same name and keeps the rest, including `env`, `headers`, and `auth`. For example, this turns off a user-level server in one project:\n35\t\n36\t```json\n37\t{\n38\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n39\t    \"internal-tools\": { \"enabled\": false }\n40\t  }\n41\t}\n42\t```\n43\t\n44\tThe format matches other MCP clients:\n45\t\n46\t```json\n47\t{\n48\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n49\t    \"filesystem\": {\n50\t      \"command\": \"npx\",\n51\t      \"args\": [\"-y\", \"@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem\", \".\"]\n52\t    },\n53\t    \"docs\": {\n54\t      \"url\": \"https://example.com/mcp\",\n55\t      \"headers\": { \"Authorization\": \"Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}\" },\n56\t      \"description\": \"Search and read the product documentation\"\n57\t    }\n58\t  }\n59\t}\n60\t```\n61\t\n62\tStdio servers use `command`, `args`, `env`, and `cwd`. Relative `cwd` values resolve against the session directory. A leading `~/` in `command`, an argument, or `cwd` names the home directory.\n63\t\n64\tHTTP servers use `url`, `headers`, and `oauth` (see [Authenticate with OAuth](#authenticate-with-oauth)). The legacy SSE transport is not supported.\n65\t\n66\tBoth server types support:\n67\t\n68\t- `timeout`: per-request timeout in seconds (default 60). Progress notifications reset it.\n69\t- `enabled: false`: keep the entry without connecting to it.\n70\t- `exposure` and `toolExposure`: control how tools reach the model (see [Control tool exposure](#control-tool-exposure)).\n71\t- `description`: what the server offers, in a sentence. It lists the server in the system prompt (see [Control tool exposure](#control-tool-exposure)), tool search ranks the server's tools by it, and codemode's `describeNamespace()` returns it. Without it, the first line of the server instructions is used once the server connects.\n72\t\n73\tKeep personal servers and servers with credentials in the user-level file. Use the project file only for servers the project requires, and only in trusted projects.\n74\t\n75\t### Configuration rules\n76\t\n77\t- Server names may contain only letters, digits, `_`, and `-`. Tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, with every character other than letters, digits, and `_` replaced by `_`; tools of a server whose names then collide all get a hash suffix. Server names that differ only in `-` and `_` count as the same server: a second one is rejected, and a `mcp.json` server overrides a registered one.\n78\t- `type` is optional. A `command` selects stdio and a `url` selects streamable HTTP. When present, `type` must be `stdio`, `http`, or `streamable-http`.\n79\t- `sse` is rejected. Servers that document an SSE endpoint often also provide streamable HTTP, commonly at `/mcp` instead of `/sse`.\n80\t- `command` is one executable and `args` contains its arguments. It is not a shell command string.\n81\t- `env` and `headers` values can use environment variables such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`. They can also run a command with `!command`, but the command must make up the whole value, for example `\"Authorization\": \"!echo Bearer $(gh auth token)\"`.\n82\t- Invalid entries are reported and skipped without preventing other servers from connecting.\n83\t\n84\t`pi mcp add` and `pi mcp remove` cover common changes from a shell. See [MCP commands](cli.md#mcp-commands) for their options.\n85\t\n86\t### Inspect or change a server\n87\t\n88\t`/mcp` lists configured servers with their state, tool count, exposure, and configuration source. Servers that need attention appear first. Select a server to inspect its tools and connection details, reconnect, sign in or out, change exposure, or enable and disable it.\n89\t\n90\tExposure and enabled-state changes are saved to the file that defines the server without replacing unrelated content. In a trusted project, \"Enable in this project\" and \"Disable in this project\" add a project override for a user-level server; later changes to that server are saved to the override. Disabled servers remain listed. Outside the interactive TUI, `/mcp` prints server status; `/mcp login <server>`, `/mcp logout <server>`, and `/mcp reconnect <server>` perform those actions directly.\n91\t\n92\tShell commands work without a session: `pi mcp add`, `pi mcp remove`, `pi mcp list`, `pi mcp login`, and `pi mcp logout`. Shell commands do not load extensions.\n93\t\n94\t### Diagnose connection problems\n95\t\n96\tRun `pi mcp list` to connect to every enabled server and print its state, tools, and errors. It exits with status 1 when an entry is invalid or an enabled server is not connected. `/mcp` shows the full connection error and the tail of stderr from a failed stdio server.\n97\t\n98\tPi reports configuration errors, failed connections, and required sign-ins once after startup. Server logging notifications are appended to `~/.pi/agent/mcp.log` as `<time> [<server>] <level> <logger>: <message>`. The file moves to `mcp.log.1` after it grows past 5 MB.\n99\t\n100\tPi connects every enabled server in the background when a session starts. A server's tools appear once it connects; the `codemode` description does not list them, so it does not change when servers connect. The first prompt waits up to 10 seconds only for servers with `direct` tools, which must be declared in its request. Other servers are waited for when they are needed: a codemode script waits for the servers it names (`mcp__<server>`) and, when it calls `searchTools()` or reads `ALL_TOOLS`, for all of them; `tool_search` and the resource tools also wait for all of them. HTTP network errors and transient statuses (408, 429, and 5xx) are retried twice. A dropped connection is shown as disconnected and reconnects on the next call. When a server announces a changed tool list, new tools are added and withdrawn tools become unreachable.\n101\t\n102\tStopping a stdio server closes its stdin, sends SIGTERM, then sends SIGKILL to its process group. This also stops servers launched through wrappers such as `npx` or `uvx`.\n103\t\n104\t## Migrate configuration from another client\n105\t\n106\tMove the converted entry under `mcpServers` in `mcp.json`, then run `pi mcp list` to validate it.\n107\t\n108\t| Client | Conversion |\n109\t|---|---|\n110\t| Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or Cursor | Copy the existing `mcpServers` entry. |\n111\t| VS Code | Move an entry from the top-level `servers` object and replace `${input:...}` prompts with `${NAME}` environment variables. |\n112\t| Codex | Convert `[mcp_servers.<name>]` TOML fields such as `command`, `args`, `env`, and `url` to JSON. |\n113\t| OpenCode | Convert `\"type\": \"local\"` to a stdio entry, split its `command` array into `command` and `args`, rename `environment` to `env`, and replace `{env:NAME}` with `${NAME}`. Convert `\"type\": \"remote\"` to a URL entry. |\n114\t\n115\t## Authenticate with OAuth\n116\t\n117\tRemote servers that use OAuth, such as Sentry, need no credentials in `mcp.json`:\n118\t\n119\t```json\n120\t{\n121\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n122\t    \"sentry\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp\" }\n123\t  }\n124\t}\n125\t```\n126\t\n127\tWhen the server rejects an unauthenticated connection, `/mcp` shows that it needs sign-in. Select \"Sign in\", run `/mcp login sentry`, or run `pi mcp login sentry`. Pi opens the authorization page and waits for approval. If the browser runs on another machine, such as over SSH, paste its redirected URL into the sign-in screen. A running session uses the new credentials on its next turn.\n128\t\n129\tPi registers itself with the authorization server, stores tokens in `~/.pi/agent/mcp-auth.json`, and refreshes access tokens when they expire or the server rejects them. If a server later requests additional scope, Pi asks for sign-in again. Signing out deletes the stored credentials.\n130\t\n131\tCredentials belong to a server name and URL. Servers with the same URL under different names, such as one per account, sign in separately; servers with the same name and URL in different `mcp.json` files share one sign-in.\n132\t\n133\tOAuth applies to HTTP servers without an `Authorization` header. For a server that does not support dynamic client registration, configure a registered client:\n134\t\n135\t```json\n136\t{\n137\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n138\t    \"example\": {\n139\t      \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\",\n140\t      \"oauth\": { \"clientId\": \"my-client\", \"clientSecret\": \"${EXAMPLE_SECRET}\", \"callbackPort\": 8765 }\n141\t    }\n142\t  }\n143\t}\n144\t```\n145\t\n146\tThe redirect URI must match the registered URI. `callbackPort` uses `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. To use another URI, set `callbackUrl`; it must use HTTP on `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`. Pi sends it exactly as written. When `callbackUrl` omits a port, Pi uses `callbackPort` or a free port and adds it to the URI, as allowed for loopback redirects by RFC 8252. `clientSecret` is optional and can use an environment variable or command.\n147\t\n148\tSet `scope` to a space-separated list for servers that do not advertise their required scopes. Otherwise, Pi requests the advertised scopes. Later scope requests are added to the configured value.\n149\t\n150\tPi registers as `pi`. Some servers only accept registrations from known clients. Set `clientName` to send another name:\n151\t\n152\t```json\n153\t{\n154\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n155\t    \"figma\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.figma.com/mcp\", \"oauth\": { \"clientName\": \"Claude Code\" } }\n156\t  }\n157\t}\n158\t```\n159\t\n160\tThe name is only sent when Pi registers a client. To register again under a new name, sign out first.\n161\t\n162\tSome authorization servers allow clients by their Client ID Metadata Document URL instead of registering them. Set `clientRegistration` to `cimd` to identify as Pi's document on pi.dev instead of registering:\n163\t\n164\t```json\n165\t{\n166\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n167\t    \"example\": { \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\", \"oauth\": { \"clientRegistration\": \"cimd\" } }\n168\t  }\n169\t}\n170\t```\n171\t\n172\tThe client ID is `https://pi.dev/oauth/client.json` with the redirect URI `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. If the authorization server does not send the `iss` parameter in authorization responses (RFC 9207), Pi uses a document and redirect path specific to the MCP server instead: `https://pi.dev/oauth/<id>/client.json` with `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback/<id>`. The authorization server must advertise Client ID Metadata Document support and public clients, or sign-in fails. `cimd` cannot be combined with `clientId` or `clientName`, and a `callbackUrl` must use `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` with the path `/callback`.\n173\t\n174\tPi finds the authorization server through the server's protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) and checks that the authorization server's metadata names the expected issuer (RFC 8414). Some servers advertise the wrong authorization server or none, so sign-in opens a page that does not exist. Set `authServerMetadataUrl` to the metadata document of the right authorization server:\n175\t\n176\t```json\n177\t{\n178\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n179\t    \"example\": {\n180\t      \"url\": \"https://mcp.example.com/mcp\",\n181\t      \"oauth\": { \"authServerMetadataUrl\": \"https://example.okta.com/.well-known/openid-configuration\" }\n182\t    }\n183\t  }\n184\t}\n185\t```\n186\t\n187\tPi uses that document instead of discovery and trusts it as configured, so only point it at a document you trust. The URL must use HTTPS, except on `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`.\n188\t\n189\t## Control tool exposure\n190\t\n191\tEach server tool is registered as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. The server's `exposure` determines how the model reaches it:\n192\t\n193\t| Exposure | Behavior | Typical use |\n194\t|---|---|---|\n195\t| `codemode` (default) | Callable from [`codemode`](cli.md#tools) scripts, but neither declared to the model nor listed in the codemode description. Scripts find tools with `searchTools()`, `describeTool()`, or `ALL_TOOLS`. | General MCP servers, especially when scripts should combine or filter calls. |\n196\t| `deferred` | Not declared until [`tool_search`](cli.md#tools) loads a match for the next model call. | Large servers whose tools should be called directly after discovery. |\n197\t| `direct` | Declared to the model like a built-in tool and also callable from codemode. | Small, frequently used tool sets. |\n198\t| `hidden` | Registered but unreachable. | Servers or tools that should remain unavailable. |\n199\t\n200\t`codemode-deferred` is accepted as an alias for `codemode`.\n201\t\n202\tServers with `codemode` or `deferred` tools are listed in the `mcp_servers` section of the system prompt, with how their tools are reached and one line from the configured `description` or, once connected, from the server instructions. Pi updates the section when a prompt starts, after waiting for servers with `direct` tools. When it changed, for example because a server connected and its summary became available, Pi appends the new section to the conversation instead of changing tool declarations, so earlier messages stay cached. `describeNamespace()` and the `namespace` option of `searchTools()` accept `mcp__dev-radius`, `mcp__dev_radius`, `dev-radius`, or `dev_radius`.\n203\t\n204\tPi activates `codemode` when a server with `codemode` exposure connects. It activates `tool_search` for a server with `deferred` exposure. To make the model see a tool without searching, give it `direct` exposure with `toolExposure`.\n205\t\n206\t`toolExposure` overrides the server exposure for individual tools. Keys are exact server tool names or patterns where `*` matches any characters. Exact names win over patterns; among patterns, the first match wins. A server with `hidden` exposure can expose only selected tools:\n207\t\n208\t```json\n209\t{\n210\t  \"mcpServers\": {\n211\t    \"github\": {\n212\t      \"url\": \"https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/\",\n213\t      \"exposure\": \"deferred\",\n214\t      \"toolExposure\": {\n215\t        \"search_code\": \"direct\",\n216\t        \"get_*\": \"codemode\",\n217\t        \"delete_*\": \"hidden\"\n218\t      }\n219\t    }\n220\t  }\n221\t}\n222\t```\n223\t\n224\t`pi mcp list` marks tools whose exposure differs from their server. The Tools view in `/mcp` also shows the effective exposure.\n225\t\n226\tTools with `codemode` or `deferred` exposure can be reached through either indirect mechanism: codemode scripts can call them, and `tool_search` can load them. Codemode calls do not depend on the active tool set, so they remain available after `/tree`, resume, and fork. Tools loaded by `tool_search` are recorded in the transcript and remain declared on that branch.\n227\t\n228\tTo keep `codemode` active without MCP servers, add `\"defaultTools\": [\"+codemode\"]` to [settings](settings.md#tools). To prevent automatic codemode activation, set `\"autoEnableCodemode\": false` beside `mcpServers`. A project value overrides the user-level value. Pi warns once when neither `codemode` nor `tool_search` is active and non-direct tools cannot be called.\n229\t\n230\tText results over 20 KB reach the model with their middle removed around a `…N chars truncated…` marker. The full text is saved to a temporary file named in the result. Codemode scripts receive the complete result and can reduce it before returning output to the model.\n231\t\n232\tCodemode scripts receive the complete MCP `CallToolResult`, including `content`, `structuredContent`, and `isError`. A result with `isError` resolves inside scripts but is reported as an error for direct calls. `image(result.content[0])` forwards an image block. Server instructions are not part of any tool description; scripts read them with `describeNamespace(\"mcp__<server>\")`, which also returns the server's tool names.\n233\t\n234\t## Use resources\n235\t\n236\tWhen a connected server offers [resources](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/resources), Pi adds the resource tools used by Codex and OpenCode:\n237\t\n238\t- `list_mcp_resources` lists resources as JSON: `{ server?, resources: [{ server, uri, name, ... }], nextCursor? }`. With `server`, it lists one page; `cursor` continues with the next page. Without `server`, it lists every resource from every server.\n239\t- `list_mcp_resource_templates` lists URI templates for resources the servers do not list directly.\n240\t- `read_mcp_resource` reads a resource by `server` and `uri`. Text reaches the model as text and images as images. Other binary resources are saved to temporary files, and the model receives the path. Scripts receive `{ server, uri, contents }`.\n241\t\n242\tThese tools reach every enabled, non-hidden server with resources. Their exposure is the widest exposure among those servers: `direct`, then `codemode` or `deferred`. Resource links in tool results identify `read_mcp_resource` and the server.\n243\t\n244\tResources for MCP Apps, identified by `ui://` URIs or `text/html;profile=mcp-app`, are omitted because Pi does not render them. Resource icons are also omitted.\n245\t\n246\tReading and listing resources is retried once after a transient HTTP error (408, 429, or 5xx). Tool calls are not retried because the server may already have performed them.\n247\t\n248\t## Permissions\n249\t\n250\tEvery MCP call passes through Pi's tool pipeline. Extension `tool_call` and `tool_result` handlers, including permission gates, therefore apply to MCP tools. Calls made from codemode scripts carry the codemode call ID as `parentToolCallId`.\n251\t\n252\t`pi.getAllTools()` reports the annotations declared by each server: `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, and `openWorldHint`. Permission extensions can use these hints to decide which calls require confirmation (see [Tool exposure](extensions.md#tool-exposure)). Resource tools are marked read-only.\n253\t\n254\t## Extensions and SDK\n255\t\n256\t### Add servers from extensions\n257\t\n258\tExtensions can add servers for the current session with `pi.registerMcpServer(name, config)`, using the same shape as an `mcpServers` entry (see [MCP servers in extensions](extensions.md#mcp-servers)). Registered servers connect like configured servers and appear in `/mcp` with the extension as their source.\n259\t\n260\tChanges to enabled state or exposure apply only to the current session. A file-configured server with the same name takes precedence, and `/mcp` lists the overridden registration. `pi mcp` shell commands do not load extensions and only see file-configured servers.\n261\t\n262\t### Replace the built-in MCP support\n263\t\n264\tAn installed extension that registers `/mcp`, such as `pi-mcp-adapter`, replaces the built-in MCP support for sessions. Pi then does not read `mcp.json` or connect its servers in a session, and `/mcp` belongs to the extension. Remove the extension to restore the built-in behavior. To disable built-in MCP support without a replacement, disable `mcp` under Built-in in `pi config`, or set `\"extensions\": [\"-builtin:mcp\"]` in [settings](settings.md#resources).\n265\t\n266\tAn extension that registers `codemode` or `tool_search` similarly replaces the built-in tool with that name. Shell-level `pi mcp` commands always use the built-in implementation.\n267\t\n268\t### Use MCP from the SDK\n269\t\n270\tSDK sessions do not load built-in extensions. Add the MCP extension, the codemode extension for `codemode` servers, and the tool-search extension for `deferred` servers to the resource loader. Retry reconnects and refreshes model state without replaying the interrupted operation.\n88\t\n89\t## Classification\n90\t\n91\tEvery model listed for chat is also listed as a classifier model with the same ID and the `llama-cpp-classify` API. Classifier models answer typed `choice`, `bool`, and `score` questions about JSON state, like TypeSafe's Jev models. The model reaches them from [`codemode`](cli.md#enable-codemode) scripts, and extensions through `ctx.modelRegistry.classify()`; see [Classifier models](models.md#use-classifier-models).\n92\t\n93\tThe model does not generate an answer. Each question becomes one chat prompt: the state, every question of the request, the state again, and then the question with its answers under single-token labels. Labels are letters for a choice (up to 62 options), `Yes`/`No` for a bool, and digits for a score (up to 10 levels). The second copy of the state is read with the questions in view, which improved accuracy on JevBench with small models. Pi reads the probabilities of the labels as the next token and normalizes them. A choice returns every option's probability and a confidence of `(n * peak - 1) / (n - 1)`; a score returns the expected level.\n94\t\n95\t- Raw label probabilities are usually overconfident. The per-request `temperature` option divides the label logits before normalizing; values above 1 soften the distribution. It changes no answer.\n96\t- Questions run one after another. Everything before the final question is the same for all questions of a request, so the server's prompt cache evaluates it once. The state appears twice, so it needs twice its size in context.\n97\t- Small models may follow instructions written inside the state. The prompt tells the model to judge the state as data, but that is not a guarantee.\n98\t- Hybrid models such as Qwen3.5 cannot rewind a partially cached prompt without context checkpoints. If each question reprocesses the whole state, start the router with `--ctx-checkpoints 32 --checkpoint-min-step 0`.\n99\t\n100\t## Troubleshooting\n101\t\n102\tCheck that the router is reachable:\n103\t\n104\t```bash\n105\tcurl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health\n106\tcurl http://127.0.0.1:8080/models\n107\t```\n108\t\n109\t- **No models in `/llama`:** Check `--models-dir`, the directory layout, and restart the router.\n110\t- **Model missing from `/model` with `--no-models-autoload`:** Load it with `/llama` first.\n111\t- **Load fails or uses too much memory:** Lower `-c` or unload another model.\n112\t- **Server is not in router mode:** Start it without `--model`, `-m`, or `-hf`.\n113\t\n114\tTo remove the `llama.cpp` provider and `/llama`, disable `llama.cpp` under Built-in in `pi config`, or set `\"extensions\": [\"-builtin:llama.cpp\"]` in [settings](settings.md#resources).\n115\t"}]}}

Use custom model configuration only when Pi does not already include the provider or endpoint you need.\n\n## Choose a connection\n\n| What you have | Recommended setup |\n|---|---|\n| A supported subscription | Sign in through `/login` |\n| A provider API key | Store it through `/login` or set its environment variable |\n| A local GGUF model | Connect Pi to the llama.cpp router |\n| An OpenAI-, Anthropic-, or Google-compatible endpoint | Add it to `models.json` |\n| A provider with a custom protocol or authentication flow | Build or install a provider extension |\n\nBrowse the [model catalog](https://pi.dev/models) for current providers, model IDs, capabilities, context limits, and pricing. Pi starts with its bundled catalog and can overlay newer catalog data from pi.dev. Cached catalog data remains available offline; run `pi update --models` to force a refresh.\n\n## Authenticate\n\nRun `/login` and select a provider. Pi stores credentials in [`auth.json`](configuration.md#agent-directory). Run `/logout` to remove stored credentials for a provider.\n\nYou can instead provide an API key through the provider's environment variable. This is useful in CI and other environments where Pi should not write credentials. [Providers](providers.md) lists the variables and provider-specific setup.\n\nWhen several credential sources are configured, Pi uses a runtime `--api-key` first, then a stored `auth.json` credential, an `apiKey` from `models.json`, and finally the provider's environment variables or ambient cloud credentials. Provider extensions can define their own authentication behavior.\n\nKeep `auth.json` and any credential commands private. Project settings and extensions can execute inside the Pi process after you trust a project. Review [Security](security.md) before loading configuration from an untrusted directory.\n\n## Select a model\n\nRun `/model` to search available models. The picker shows models whose providers have usable authentication. Press `Ctrl+S` on a model to save it as the default for new sessions.\n\nRun `/thinking` to select the thinking level for the current model. Press `Ctrl+S` there to save the startup level. Pi limits the choices to levels supported by the selected model.\n\n`Ctrl+P` cycles through available models. Use `/scoped-models` to control that cycle and save the selection, or configure model patterns through [Settings](settings.md#model-cycling).\n\nA session records model and thinking-level changes. Resuming the session restores them without changing defaults for new sessions.\n\n## Connect local models\n\nPi integrates directly with the llama.cpp router. The router discovers GGUF files and loads models on demand. Pi's `/llama` command manages the router, while `/model` selects one of its loaded models.\n\nFollow [Local Models with llama.cpp](llama-cpp.md) for server startup, model layout, downloads, and connection troubleshooting.\n\nFor Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, SGLang, and other compatible servers, [configure a compatible endpoint](#configure-a-compatible-endpoint) in `models.json`.\n\n## Configure a compatible endpoint\n\nUse [`models.json`](configuration.md#agent-directory) when an endpoint speaks an API Pi already supports. This includes most Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, SGLang, and proxy deployments.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"providers\": {\n    \"ollama\": {\n      \"baseUrl\": \"http://localhost:11434/v1\",\n      \"api\": \"openai-completions\",\n      \"apiKey\": \"ollama\",\n      \"models\": [\n        { \"id\": \"qwen2.5-coder:7b\" }\n      ]\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe dummy key makes the model available to Pi; Ollama ignores it. For an authenticated endpoint, `apiKey` and header values can use `$NAME` or `${NAME}` environment interpolation, a literal value, or a leading `!command`. Commands in `models.json` run at request time and are not cached by Pi.\n\nOpening `/model` reloads the file. A `models` entry adds or replaces a model with the same ID on that provider. Use `modelOverrides` to change metadata for an existing built-in or extension-provided model without replacing the provider's model list. Unknown override IDs are ignored.\n\n### Describe model input and caching\n\nUse `inputLimits.images.resize` to control how Pi encodes new image attachments, `read` results, and tool-result images before storing them in conversation history:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"vision-model\",\n  \"input\": [\"text\", \"image\"],\n  \"inputLimits\": {\n    \"images\": {\n      \"resize\": {\n        \"maxWidth\": 1568,\n        \"maxHeight\": 1568,\n        \"maxBytes\": 524288,\n        \"jpegQuality\": 75\n      }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\n`maxBytes` limits the base64-encoded payload. Omitted resize fields use conservative defaults of 2000 by 2000 pixels, 4.5 MiB encoded, and JPEG quality 80. Images are encoded once; changing models does not rewrite historical images. The catalog can also describe hard request limits with `inputLimits.maxRequestBytes`, `images.maxPerMessage`, and `images.maxPerRequest`, but Pi does not yet rewrite or reject history based on them.\n\n<a id=\"prompt-cache-lifetimes\"></a>\n\nUse `promptCache` to declare the provider's best-effort cache lifetime in seconds for the `short` or `long` retention tier:\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"claude-sonnet-5\", \"promptCache\": { \"short\": 300, \"long\": 3600 } }\n```\n\nChoose the conservative end of any published range. A model without a lifetime for the active tier is not eligible for cache warming. A `modelOverrides` entry can set `inputLimits` or `promptCache` for a built-in or extension model, including a model accessed through a validated proxy. See [`cacheWarming`](settings.md#model-and-thinking).\n\n### Configure sampling by thinking level\n\nOpenAI-compatible APIs support free-form `samplingParams` model defaults and `samplingParamsByThinkingLevel` overrides. The latter uses Pi thinking-level keys (`off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`), not provider values from `thinkingLevelMap`:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"qwen-thinking-model\",\n  \"reasoning\": true,\n  \"samplingParams\": {\n    \"temperature\": 1.0,\n    \"top_p\": 0.95\n  },\n  \"samplingParamsByThinkingLevel\": {\n    \"off\": {\n      \"temperature\": 0.7,\n      \"top_p\": 0.8\n    },\n    \"high\": {\n      \"top_k\": 20\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nPi first clamps unsupported thinking levels, then merges model `samplingParams`, the effective level's override, and request-level `samplingParams` in that order. Later values win per key. Missing levels inherit the model defaults. `modelOverrides` merges per-level entries per key with the base model. These fields apply only to `openai-completions`, `openai-responses`, and `azure-openai-responses`; other APIs ignore them.\n\nCompatibility settings should describe verified differences in the endpoint's request or response behavior. Do not enable them based only on an endpoint advertising OpenAI or Anthropic compatibility.\n\n## Use classifier models\n\nClassifier models do not chat. They answer typed questions about JSON state: pick one of several choices, answer yes or no, or give a score, each with probabilities. Pi includes TypeSafe's Jev model from these providers, and Cloudflare's Clef and Clef Flash models from Workers AI:\n\n| Provider | Model IDs | Authentication |\n|---|---|---|\n| `typesafe` | `jev-latest` | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` |\n| `openrouter` | `typesafe/jev-1.13`, `~typesafe/jev-latest` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` or `/login` |\n| `cloudflare-workers-ai` | `typesafe/jev`, `@cf/cloudflare/clef`, `@cf/cloudflare/clef-flash` | `CLOUDFLARE_API_KEY` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` |\n| `vercel-ai-gateway` | `typesafe-ai/jev` | `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` |\n| `opencode` | `jev-1.13`, `jev-1.13-free` | `OPENCODE_API_KEY` |","is_error":false}]},"uuid":"50dd6486-5cf8-4248-85a9-62d6982c08bf","timestamp":"2026-11-04T05:59:48.963Z","toolUseResult":{"stdout":"# Choose a Model\n\nFor a built-in provider, start with `/login`, then choose a model with `/model`. Unknown override IDs are ignored.\n\n### Describe model input and caching\n\nUse `inputLimits.images.resize` to control how Pi encodes new image attachments, `read` results, and tool-result images before storing them in conversation history:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"vision-model\",\n  \"input\": [\"text\", \"image\"],\n  \"inputLimits\": {\n    \"images\": {\n      \"resize\": {\n        \"maxWidth\": 1568,\n        \"maxHeight\": 1568,\n        \"maxBytes\": 524288,\n        \"jpegQuality\": 75\n      }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\n`maxBytes` limits the base64-encoded payload. Omitted resize fields use conservative defaults of 2000 by 2000 pixels, 4.5 MiB encoded, and JPEG quality 80. Images are encoded once; changing models does not rewrite historical images. The catalog can also describe hard request limits with `inputLimits.maxRequestBytes`, `images.maxPerMessage`, and `images.maxPerRequest`, but Pi does not yet rewrite or reject history based on them.\n\n<a id=\"prompt-cache-lifetimes\"></a>\n\nUse `promptCache` to declare the provider's best-effort cache lifetime in seconds for the `short` or `long` retention tier:\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"claude-sonnet-5\", \"promptCache\": { \"short\": 300, \"long\": 3600 } }\n```\n\nChoose the conservative end of any published range. A model without a lifetime for the active tier is not eligible for cache warming. A `modelOverrides` entry can set `inputLimits` or `promptCache` for a built-in or extension model, including a model accessed through a validated proxy. See [`cacheWarming`](settings.md#model-and-thinking).\n\n### Configure sampling by thinking level\n\nOpenAI-compatible APIs support free-form `samplingParams` model defaults and `samplingParamsByThinkingLevel` overrides. The latter uses Pi thinking-level keys (`off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`), not provider values from `thinkingLevelMap`:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"qwen-thinking-model\",\n  \"reasoning\": true,\n  \"samplingParams\": {\n    \"temperature\": 1.0,\n    \"top_p\": 0.95\n  },\n  \"samplingParamsByThinkingLevel\": {\n    \"off\": {\n      \"temperature\": 0.7,\n      \"top_p\": 0.8\n    },\n    \"high\": {\n      \"top_k\": 20\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nPi first clamps unsupported thinking levels, then merges model `samplingParams`, the effective level's override, and request-level `samplingParams` in that order. Later values win per key. Missing levels inherit the model defaults. `modelOverrides` merges per-level entries per key with the base model. These fields apply only to `openai-completions`, `openai-responses`, and `azure-openai-responses`; other APIs ignore them.\n\nCompatibility settings should describe verified differences in the endpoint's request or response behavior. Do not enable them based only on an endpoint advertising OpenAI or Anthropic compatibility.\n\n## Use classifier models\n\nClassifier models do not chat. Setup\n\n| Item | Value |\n| :--- | :--- |\n| Model | Qwen3.5-4B GGUF served by `llama-server` at `http://127.0.0.1:8080` (record the exact file from `doctor`) |\n| Context window | read from `llama-server /props` (per slot), passed to Pi as `contextWindow` |\n| Agent | Pi (`pi --print --mode json`), default tools `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write` |\n| Pi config | a fresh, isolated `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` per run: no user MCP servers, skills, prompt templates, themes, or context files |\n| Compaction | on, `reserveTokens` 4096, `keepRecentTokens` 8000 (the default 16384 reserve is too large for a ~30K window) |\n| Test runner | `eval/work/venv` (Python 3.12 + pytest), first on the agent's `PATH` |\n| Timeout | 30 minutes per run |\n\n**What differs in acc mode (the treatment):**\n- ACC-MCP is added as a stdio MCP server with `direct` exposure, so its four tools (`mcp__acc_mcp__get_adaptive_context`, `find_symbol`, `get_token_ledger`, `reset_session`) are declared to the model like built-in tools.\n- `ACC_MCP_ROOT` is the task workspace, `ACC_MCP_LEDGER` is a per-run file outside it, and the session budget is 6,000 tokens.\n- One sentence is appended to the system prompt telling the model to prefer these tools for reading code (`ACC_HINT` in `pi_bench.py`). Run with `--no-hint` to measure the tools without it.\n\nThe built-in `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write` tools stay available in both modes, so acc mode can always fall back to reading files.\n\n## 3. Grading\n\nAfter the run:\n1. The agent's patch is saved (`patch.diff`), and whether it touched `tests/` is recorded.\n2. `tests/` is restored to the original, so editing tests cannot help.\n3. **Resolved** = the target tests pass, and the full test suite has no failures beyond those already failing on the clean repo (recorded by `validate`).\n\n## 4. Metrics\n\nFrom Pi's JSON events (`events.jsonl`):\n\n| Metric | Meaning |\n| :--- | :--- |\n| Model calls | assistant responses (one per agent step) |\n| Peak context | largest prompt of one model call (input + cached tokens, as llama-server reports them) |\n| Prompt tokens | sum of prompts over all calls: the total context the model had to process |\n| Output tokens | generated tokens |\n| Tool calls / tool output | calls and characters returned per tool |\n| Compactions | times Pi had to summarize the conversation to fit the window |\n\nFrom the ACC-MCP ledger (acc mode): requests, served tier per request, model tier, `min_tier` escalations, budget step-downs, tokens served vs whole-file tokens, and refused requests.\n\n## 5. Running\n\nRun these from the repository root (the model must already be running on port 8080):\n\n```bash\nuv sync                                   # ACC-MCP itself must be importable from .venv\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py setup            # clone repos, create eval/work/venv\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py validate         # all 10 tasks must be OK\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py doctor           # acc-mcp must show \"connected, 4 tools\"\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py run --tasks mi_difference      # one task, both modes: a quick smoke test\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py run              # all tasks, both modes\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py report           # writes eval/results.md\n```\n\nEverything a run produces is under `eval/work/runs/<run-id>/<mode>/<task>/` (`events.jsonl`, Pi session, `acc_ledger.json`, `patch.diff`, JUnit reports, `result.json`).\n\n## 6. Limits\n\n- 10 tasks and one run per task and mode: a difference of one or two tasks is noise, not a result. The runner is [`pi_bench.py`](pi_bench.py); the tasks are in [`tasks.json`](tasks.json); results go to `results.md`.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Question\n\nDoes giving a small local model ACC-MCP change **whether it can fix a bug in real code** and **how much context it uses doing so**, when the model works inside a real coding agent?\n\n- **H1 (context):** with ACC-MCP, the agent's prompts are smaller (lower peak context per model call and fewer total prompt tokens per task), because it reads signature, call-graph, or single-function slices instead of whole files.\n- **H2 (success):** with ACC-MCP, the agent resolves at least as many tasks as without it, because the slices it gets still contain what it needs.\n\nBoth hypotheses are checked on the same tasks, so each task gives a paired comparison.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Why our own benchmark\n\n| Option | Why not used |\n| :--- | :--- |\n| SWE-bench / SWE-bench Lite | The official grader builds a Docker image per task (several GB each; built locally on Apple Silicon). Too heavy for a 16 GB laptop that also runs the model, and the large repos (Django, sympy) are far beyond a 4B model. |\n| Aider / Exercism Python exercises | Each task is one small file. Reading the whole file is cheap, so ACC-MCP has nothing to save and the comparison would only test the agent. |\n| HumanEval / MBPP | Single functions with no repository. There is nothing to navigate, so an MCP server for code context is irrelevant. |\n\nWhat the comparison needs is **real, popular code with files large enough that reading them whole is expensive or impossible**, plus **tests that decide pass/fail automatically without Docker**. The benchmark therefore injects bugs into pinned releases of two well-known pure-Python libraries and grades with their own test suites. This is the bug-injection approach used by SWE-smith: take a working repository, break one function, and ask the agent to repair it from a bug report.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Repositories\n\n| | more-itertools | click |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| Source | https://github.com/more-itertools/more-itertools | https://github.com/pallets/click |\n| Pinned release | tag `v11.2.1` | tag `8.5.0` |\n| License | MIT | BSD-3-Clause |\n| What it is | Extra iterator building blocks on top of `itertools` | Command-line interface framework (Pallets) |\n| Runtime dependencies | none | none (on macOS/Linux) |\n| Package layout | `more_itertools/` at the repo root | `src/click/` (tests need `PYTHONPATH=src`) |\n| Test suite | `tests/`, `unittest.TestCase` classes, run with pytest | `tests/`, plain pytest |\n| Files with injected bugs | `more_itertools/more.py`: 5,644 lines, ~175 KB | `src/click/core.py`: 3,799 lines; `types.py`: 1,422; `parser.py`: 533; `formatting.py`: 320 |\n| Why chosen | `more.py` is about 45K tokens, **larger than the model's ~30K context window**: the agent cannot read it whole and has to find the right function. Hundreds of small, independent functions. | Real class hierarchy (`Command`, `Parameter`, `Option`, `HelpFormatter`) with code split across modules, so callers and callees matter (Tier 2). `core.py` alone is also larger than a comfortable read. |\n\nBoth repos are cloned shallowly at the pinned tag (`setup`). Sizes are for these tags.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Tasks\n\n### 4.1 How the tasks were built\n\n1. Pick a function in one of the files above that has its own tests in the repository.\n2. Change **one line or one condition** so the function gives wrong results but the code still imports and runs: a swapped argument order, an off-by-one comparison, a flipped condition.\n3. Spread the tasks through the files (start, middle, end of `more.py`; four different click modules), so no task is solved by reading the first lines of a file.\n4. Write a **bug report** the way a user would file it: what they called, what they got, what they expected. Reports for more-itertools name the public function, as a user would. Reports for click describe only the user-visible behavior and never name the internal function. No report mentions a file, a line, or the code change.\n5. Record the tests that cover the function as the task's **target tests**.\n6. Check with `validate` that the target tests pass on the original code and fail with the bug (section 4.3).\n\n### 4.2 Task catalogue\n\n| Task | Repo | File (line) | Function | Injected change | Target tests | Bug report (summary) |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| `mi_split_at` | more-itertools | `more.py` (1600) | `split_at` | `if maxsplit == 1:` → `if maxsplit == 2:` | `SplitAtTests` | `maxsplit=2` splits only once; `maxsplit=1` never stops |\n| `mi_numeric_range_index` | more-itertools | `more.py` (2476) | `numeric_range.index` | `self._start >= value > self._stop` → `self._start > value > self._stop` | `NumericRangeTests` | `.index()` of the first item of a decreasing range raises `ValueError` |\n| `mi_difference` | more-itertools | `more.py` (2940) | `difference` | `map(func, b, a)` → `map(func, a, b)` | `DifferenceTest` | differences come out negated / wrong for custom functions |\n| `mi_is_sorted` | more-itertools | `more.py` (4079) | `is_sorted` | strict and non-strict checks swapped | `IsSortedTests` | `is_sorted([1, 2, 2])` is `False`, with `strict=True` it is `True` |\n| `mi_constrained_batches` | more-itertools | `more.py` (4981) | `constrained_batches` | `> max_size` → `>= max_size` | `ConstrainedBatchesTests` | items that exactly fill `max_size` are split into two batches |\n| `ck_nargs_tuple` | click | `parser.py` (90) | `_unpack_args` | `if spos is not None:` → `if spos is None:` before `x.reverse()` | `test_arguments.py::test_nargs_tup` | `nargs=2` arguments arrive reversed |\n| `ck_int_range_min` | click | `types.py` (664) | `_NumberRangeBase.convert` | `operator.le if self.min_open else operator.lt` → the two operators swapped | `test_types.py::test_range` | `IntRange(5)` rejects `5`; `min_open=True` accepts the bound |\n| `ck_eager_order` | click | `core.py` (164) | `iter_params_for_processing` | `return not item.is_eager, idx` → `return item.is_eager, idx` | `test_commands.py::test_iter_params_for_processing` | eager options (`--version`, `--help`) run after normal ones |\n| `ck_envvar_nargs` | click | `core.py` (2725) | `Parameter.value_from_envvar` | `self.nargs != 1` → `self.nargs > 1` | `test_arguments.py::test_nargs_envvar` | a `nargs=-1` argument no longer splits its environment variable |\n| `ck_help_columns` | click | `formatting.py` (255) | `HelpFormatter.write_dl` | `term_len(first) <= ...` → `term_len(first) < ...` | `test_formatting.py` | in `--help`, the longest option's description wraps to the next line |\n\nExact before/after strings and full bug reports are in `tasks.json`. more-itertools test classes are in `tests/test_more.py`.\n\n### 4.3 Validation (before any run)\n\n`python3 eval/pi_bench.py validate`:\n1. Runs each repository's full test suite on the clean code and stores the failing tests, if any, as the **baseline** (`eval/work/baseline/<repo>.json`). These are not counted against the agent later.\n2. For each task, checks that the \"before\" string occurs exactly once in the file, that the target tests pass on the clean code, and that at least one target test fails with the bug.\n\nA task that fails validation is fixed or dropped before running the benchmark.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Conditions\n\nEach task runs once in each of two modes. The **only** differences between the modes are the ACC-MCP server and one hint sentence.\n\n### 5.1 Held constant in both modes\n\n| Item | Value |\n| :--- | :--- |\n| Model | Qwen3.5-4B GGUF served by `llama-server` at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. The exact file is printed by `doctor` and must be recorded with the results. |\n| Context window | per-slot `n_ctx` read from `llama-server /props` (30,208 on the reference machine), given to Pi as the model's `contextWindow` |\n| Max output per call | 4,096 tokens |\n| Agent | Pi coding agent, non-interactive: `pi --print --mode json --offline` |\n| Tools | Pi's defaults: `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write` |\n| Pi configuration | a fresh `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` per run containing only `models.json`, `settings.json` (and `mcp.json` in acc mode). The user's own MCP servers, skills, prompt templates, themes and `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` files are not loaded (`--no-context-files --no-skills --no-prompt-templates --no-themes`). |\n| Compaction | on, `reserveTokens` 4,096, `keepRecentTokens` 8,000 (Pi's default reserve of 16,384 would leave little of a 30K window) |\n| Prompt | the same template for every task: the bug report, \"find the cause in the library source code and fix it, do not modify or add tests, you can run the tests with `python -m pytest <path>`, reply with one sentence\" |\n| Workspace | a fresh copy of the pinned repo with the bug committed as its only commit |\n| Python for the agent's commands | `eval/work/venv` (Python 3.12 + pytest), first on `PATH`; `PYTHONPATH=src` for click |\n| Time limit | 30 minutes per run; the whole process group is killed after that |\n| Order | for each task, plain then acc, so slow drift (heat, other load) affects both modes alike |\n\n### 5.2 The treatment (acc mode only)\n\n- ACC-MCP is started by Pi as a stdio MCP server (`.venv/bin/python -m acc_mcp.server`) with `direct` exposure, so its tools are declared to the model like built-in tools: `mcp__acc_mcp__get_adaptive_context`, `mcp__acc_mcp__find_symbol`, `mcp__acc_mcp__get_token_ledger`, `mcp__acc_mcp__reset_session`.\n- `ACC_MCP_ROOT` = the task workspace; `ACC_MCP_LEDGER` = a per-run file outside the workspace; session budget 6,000 tokens.\n- One sentence is appended to the system prompt (`ACC_HINT` in `pi_bench.py`): prefer `find_symbol` and `get_adaptive_context` over reading whole files, and call again with `min_tier=3` if a slice is not enough.\n- The built-in tools stay available, so the agent can always fall back to `read` and `bash`.\n\n`--no-hint` runs acc mode without the sentence, to separate the effect of the tools from the effect of the instruction.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Procedure for one run\n\n1. Copy the pinned repo into `eval/work/runs/<run-id>/<mode>/<task>/workspace/` without `.git`, apply the injected change, `git init`, commit everything as \"Initial commit\". Test caches are excluded from git via `.git/info/exclude`.\n2. Write the isolated Pi configuration for the mode (section 5).\n3. Run Pi in the workspace with the task prompt; save its JSON event stream (`events.jsonl`), its session, and stderr.\n4. When Pi exits or times out, save the agent's code changes (`patch.diff`, tests excluded) and record whether it modified anything under `tests/`.\n5. Restore `tests/` to the original, so editing tests cannot make a task pass.\n6. Run the target tests and the full test suite with JUnit reports.\n7. Compute metrics from the events and, in acc mode, from the ACC-MCP ledger.\n8. Write everything to `result.json` and delete the workspace (keep it with `--keep-workspaces`).\n\n---\n\n## 7. Grading\n\nA task is **resolved** when, after step 5:\n- every target test passes (at least one ran), and\n- the full suite has no failing test that was not already failing on the clean repo (the baseline from `validate`).\n\nAlso recorded: whether the agent changed the file that contains the bug, which files it changed, whether it edited tests, and whether the run timed out.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Metrics\n\n| Metric | Definition | Source |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| Resolved | section 7 | test runs |\n| Model calls | number of assistant responses (one per agent step) | `message_end` events |\n| Peak context | largest prompt of a single model call: input + cache-read + cache-write tokens, as llama-server reports them through Pi. Directly comparable to the context window. | `usage` of each assistant message |\n| Total prompt tokens | sum of the prompt sizes over all calls: how much context the model processed for the whole task | same |\n| Output tokens | tokens generated | same |\n| Tool calls / tool output | number of calls and characters returned, per tool | `tool_execution_end` events |\n| Compactions | times Pi had to summarize the conversation to stay in the window | `compaction_start` events |\n| Wall time | seconds from start to exit | runner |\n| ACC-MCP requests, tiers | requests served and their tier (1/2/3), and the tier the decision model picked | ACC-MCP ledger |\n| Escalations | requests where the agent raised `min_tier` above the model's tier | ACC-MCP ledger |\n| Budget step-downs / refusals | slices served one tier lower, or refused, because the session budget was nearly used up | ledger and tool output |\n| ACC-MCP tokens vs whole file | tokens served vs tokens of the whole files those slices came from | ACC-MCP ledger |\n\n---\n\n## 9. Analysis\n\n- **Per mode:** resolved count out of 10, and the median of peak context, total prompt tokens, model calls and wall time.\n- **Per task (paired):** the same task in both modes, side by side in `results.md`, so a difference can be traced to what the agent did (tools used, tiers served, escalations).\n- **Was ACC-MCP used at all?** The number of acc runs in which the model actually called an ACC-MCP tool. If a 4B model ignores the tools, the acc runs measure Pi alone, and that is itself a result.\n- With 10 tasks and one run each, a difference of one or two resolved tasks is within noise. To see the spread, repeat the whole run with a new `--run-id` and report each run, not only the best.\n- Results are reported as they come out, including if ACC-MCP makes things worse.\n\n---\n\n## 10. Threats to validity\n\n- **Small sample:** 10 tasks, one run per task and mode by default.\n- **Injected bugs:** single-line changes are easier to localize than real bugs and may not represent real maintenance work. The reports were written by the project author.\n- **Training data:** both libraries are popular and likely in the model's training data, so the model may recognize the code. This affects both modes equally but can inflate the success rate.\n- **Sampling:** the model's sampling is not seeded; reruns differ.\n- **Hint confound:** acc mode adds one instruction sentence; `--no-hint` runs separate its effect from the tools'.\n- **Token accounting:** context numbers are what llama-server reports to Pi. ACC-MCP's own counts use a different tokenizer (tiktoken or a character estimate), so its tokens and Pi's are compared only within their own source.\n- **One machine, one model:** results hold for this model file, quantization and context size.\n\n---\n\n## 11. Running it\n\nFrom the repository root, with the model already running on port 8080:\n\n```bash\nuv sync                                   # ACC-MCP must be importable from .venv\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py setup            # clone both repos at their tags, create eval/work/venv\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py validate         # baseline + all 10 tasks must be OK\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py doctor           # model, Pi version; The runner is [`pi_bench.py`](pi_bench.py); the tasks are in [`tasks.json`](tasks.json); results go to `results.md`.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Question\n\nDoes giving a small local model ACC-MCP change **whether it can fix a bug in real code** and **how much context it uses doing so**, when the model works inside a real coding agent?\n\n- **H1 (context):** with ACC-MCP, the agent's prompts are smaller (lower peak context per model call and fewer total prompt tokens per task), because it reads signature, call-graph, or single-function slices instead of whole files.\n- **H2 (success):** with ACC-MCP, the agent resolves at least as many tasks as without it, because the slices it gets still contain what it needs.\n\nBoth hypotheses are checked on the same tasks, so each task gives a paired comparison.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Why our own benchmark\n\n| Option | Why not used |\n| :--- | :--- |\n| SWE-bench / SWE-bench Lite | The official grader builds a Docker image per task (several GB each; built locally on Apple Silicon). Too heavy for a 16 GB laptop that also runs the model, and the large repos (Django, sympy) are far beyond a 4B model. |\n| Aider / Exercism Python exercises | Each task is one small file. Reading the whole file is cheap, so ACC-MCP has nothing to save and the comparison would only test the agent. |\n| HumanEval / MBPP | Single functions with no repository. There is nothing to navigate, so an MCP server for code context is irrelevant. |\n\nWhat the comparison needs is **real, popular code with files large enough that reading them whole is expensive or impossible**, plus **tests that decide pass/fail automatically without Docker**. The benchmark therefore injects bugs into pinned releases of two well-known pure-Python libraries and grades with their own test suites. This is the bug-injection approach used by SWE-smith: take a working repository, break one function, and ask the agent to repair it from a bug report.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Repositories\n\n| | more-itertools | click |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| Source | https://github.com/more-itertools/more-itertools | https://github.com/pallets/click |\n| Pinned release | tag `v11.2.1` | tag `8.5.0` |\n| License | MIT | BSD-3-Clause |\n| What it is | Extra iterator building blocks on top of `itertools` | Command-line interface framework (Pallets) |\n| Runtime dependencies | none | none (on macOS/Linux) |\n| Package layout | `more_itertools/` at the repo root | `src/click/` (tests need `PYTHONPATH=src`) |\n| Test suite | `tests/`, `unittest.TestCase` classes, run with pytest | `tests/`, plain pytest |\n| Files with injected bugs | `more_itertools/more.py`: 5,644 lines, ~175 KB | `src/click/core.py`: 3,799 lines; `types.py`: 1,422; `parser.py`: 533; `formatting.py`: 320 |\n| Why chosen | `more.py` is about 45K tokens, **larger than the model's ~30K context window**: the agent cannot read it whole and has to find the right function. Hundreds of small, independent functions. | Real class hierarchy (`Command`, `Parameter`, `Option`, `HelpFormatter`) with code split across modules, so callers and callees matter (Tier 2). `core.py` alone is also larger than a comfortable read. |\n\nBoth repos are cloned shallowly at the pinned tag (`setup`). Sizes are for these tags.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Tasks\n\n### 4.1 How the tasks were built\n\n1. Pick a function in one of the files above that has its own tests in the repository.\n2. Change **one line or one condition** so the function gives wrong results but the code still imports and runs: a swapped argument order, an off-by-one comparison, a flipped condition.\n3. Spread the tasks through the files (start, middle, end of `more.py`; four different click modules), so no task is solved by reading the first lines of a file.\n4. Write a **bug report** the way a user would file it: what they called, what they got, what they expected. Reports for more-itertools name the public function, as a user would. Reports for click describe only the user-visible behavior and never name the internal function. No report mentions a file, a line, or the code change.\n5. Record the tests that cover the function as the task's **target tests**.\n6. Check with `validate` that the target tests pass on the original code and fail with the bug (section 4.3).\n\n### 4.2 Task catalogue\n\n| Task | Repo | File (line) | Function | Injected change | Target tests | Bug report (summary) |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| `mi_split_at` | more-itertools | `more.py` (1600) | `split_at` | `if maxsplit == 1:` → `if maxsplit == 2:` | `SplitAtTests` | `maxsplit=2` splits only once; `maxsplit=1` never stops |\n| `mi_numeric_range_index` | more-itertools | `more.py` (2476) | `numeric_range.index` | `self._start >= value > self._stop` → `self._start > value > self._stop` | `NumericRangeTests` | `.index()` of the first item of a decreasing range raises `ValueError` |\n| `mi_difference` | more-itertools | `more.py` (2940) | `difference` | `map(func, b, a)` → `map(func, a, b)` | `DifferenceTest` | differences come out negated / wrong for custom functions |\n| `mi_is_sorted` | more-itertools | `more.py` (4079) | `is_sorted` | strict and non-strict checks swapped | `IsSortedTests` | `is_sorted([1, 2, 2])` is `False`, with `strict=True` it is `True` |\n| `mi_constrained_batches` | more-itertools | `more.py` (4981) | `constrained_batches` | `> max_size` → `>= max_size` | `ConstrainedBatchesTests` | items that exactly fill `max_size` are split into two batches |\n| `ck_nargs_tuple` | click | `parser.py` (90) | `_unpack_args` | `if spos is not None:` → `if spos is None:` before `x.reverse()` | `test_arguments.py::test_nargs_tup` | `nargs=2` arguments arrive reversed |\n| `ck_int_range_min` | click | `types.py` (664) | `_NumberRangeBase.convert` | `operator.le if self.min_open else operator.lt` → the two operators swapped | `test_types.py::test_range` | `IntRange(5)` rejects `5`; `min_open=True` accepts the bound |\n| `ck_eager_order` | click | `core.py` (164) | `iter_params_for_processing` | `return not item.is_eager, idx` → `return item.is_eager, idx` | `test_commands.py::test_iter_params_for_processing` | eager options (`--version`, `--help`) run after normal ones |\n| `ck_envvar_nargs` | click | `core.py` (2725) | `Parameter.value_from_envvar` | `self.nargs != 1` → `self.nargs > 1` | `test_arguments.py::test_nargs_envvar` | a `nargs=-1` argument no longer splits its environment variable |\n| `ck_help_columns` | click | `formatting.py` (255) | `HelpFormatter.write_dl` | `term_len(first) <= ...` → `term_len(first) < ...` | `test_formatting.py` | in `--help`, the longest option's description wraps to the next line |\n\nExact before/after strings and full bug reports are in `tasks.json`. more-itertools test classes are in `tests/test_more.py`.\n\n### 4.3 Validation (before any run)\n\n`python3 eval/pi_bench.py validate`:\n1. Runs each repository's full test suite on the clean code and stores the failing tests, if any, as the **baseline** (`eval/work/baseline/<repo>.json`). These are not counted against the agent later.\n2. For each task, checks that the \"before\" string occurs exactly once in the file, that the target tests pass on the clean code, and that at least one target test fails with the bug.\n\nA task that fails validation is fixed or dropped before running the benchmark.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Conditions\n\nEach task runs once in each of two modes. The **only** differences between the modes are the ACC-MCP server and one hint sentence.\n\n### 5.1 Held constant in both modes\n\n| Item | Value |\n| :--- | :--- |\n| Model | Qwen3.5-4B GGUF served by `llama-server` at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. The exact file is printed by `doctor` and must be recorded with the results. |\n| Context window | per-slot `n_ctx` read from `llama-server /props` (30,208 on the reference machine), given to Pi as the model's `contextWindow` |\n| Max output per call | 4,096 tokens |\n| Agent | Pi coding agent, non-interactive: `pi --print --mode json --offline` |\n| Tools | Pi's defaults: `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write` |\n| Pi configuration | a fresh `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` per run containing only `models.json`, `settings.json` (and `mcp.json` in acc mode). The user's own MCP servers, skills, prompt templates, themes and `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` files are not loaded (`--no-context-files --no-skills --no-prompt-templates --no-themes`). |\n| Compaction | on, `reserveTokens` 4,096, `keepRecentTokens` 8,000 (Pi's default reserve of 16,384 would leave little of a 30K window) |\n| Prompt | the same template for every task: the bug report, \"find the cause in the library source code and fix it, do not modify or add tests, you can run the tests with `python -m pytest <path>`, reply with one sentence\" |\n| Workspace | a fresh copy of the pinned repo with the bug committed as its only commit |\n| Python for the agent's commands | `eval/work/venv` (Python 3.12 + pytest), first on `PATH`; `PYTHONPATH=src` for click |\n| Time limit | 30 minutes per run; the whole process group is killed after that |\n| Order | for each task, plain then acc, so slow drift (heat, other load) affects both modes alike |\n\n### 5.2 The treatment (acc mode only)\n\n- ACC-MCP is started by Pi as a stdio MCP server (`.venv/bin/python -m acc_mcp.server`) with `direct` exposure, so its tools are declared to the model like built-in tools: `mcp__acc_mcp__get_adaptive_context`, `mcp__acc_mcp__find_symbol`, `mcp__acc_mcp__get_token_ledger`, `mcp__acc_mcp__reset_session`.\n- `ACC_MCP_ROOT` = the task workspace; `ACC_MCP_LEDGER` = a per-run file outside the workspace; session budget 6,000 tokens.\n- One sentence is appended to the system prompt (`ACC_HINT` in `pi_bench.py`): prefer `find_symbol` and `get_adaptive_context` over reading whole files, and call again with `min_tier=3` if a slice is not enough.\n- The built-in tools stay available, so the agent can always fall back to `read` and `bash`.\n\n`--no-hint` runs acc mode without the sentence, to separate the effect of the tools from the effect of the instruction.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Procedure for one run\n\n1. Copy the pinned repo into `eval/work/runs/<run-id>/<mode>/<task>/workspace/` without `.git`, apply the injected change, `git init`, commit everything as \"Initial commit\". Test caches are excluded from git via `.git/info/exclude`.\n2. Write the isolated Pi configuration for the mode (section 5).\n3. Run Pi in the workspace with the task prompt; save its JSON event stream (`events.jsonl`), its session, and stderr.\n4. When Pi exits or times out, save the agent's code changes (`patch.diff`, tests excluded) and record whether it modified anything under `tests/`.\n5. Restore `tests/` to the original, so editing tests cannot make a task pass.\n6. Run the target tests and the full test suite with JUnit reports.\n7. Compute metrics from the events and, in acc mode, from the ACC-MCP ledger.\n8. Write everything to `result.json` and delete the workspace (keep it with `--keep-workspaces`).\n\n---\n\n## 7. Grading\n\nA task is **resolved** when, after step 5:\n- every target test passes (at least one ran), and\n- the full suite has no failing test that was not already failing on the clean repo (the baseline from `validate`).\n\nAlso recorded: whether the agent changed the file that contains the bug, which files it changed, whether it edited tests, and whether the run timed out.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Metrics\n\n| Metric | Definition | Source |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| Resolved | section 7 | test runs |\n| Model calls | number of assistant responses (one per agent step) | `message_end` events |\n| Peak context | largest prompt of a single model call: input + cache-read + cache-write tokens, as llama-server reports them through Pi. Directly comparable to the context window. | `usage` of each assistant message |\n| Total prompt tokens | sum of the prompt sizes over all calls: how much context the model processed for the whole task | same |\n| Output tokens | tokens generated | same |\n| Tool calls / tool output | number of calls and characters returned, per tool | `tool_execution_end` events |\n| Compactions | times Pi had to summarize the conversation to stay in the window | `compaction_start` events |\n| Wall time | seconds from start to exit | runner |\n| ACC-MCP requests, tiers | requests served and their tier (1/2/3), and the tier the decision model picked | ACC-MCP ledger |\n| Escalations | requests where the agent raised `min_tier` above the model's tier | ACC-MCP ledger |\n| Budget step-downs / refusals | slices served one tier lower, or refused, because the session budget was nearly used up | ledger and tool output |\n| ACC-MCP tokens vs whole file | tokens served vs tokens of the whole files those slices came from | ACC-MCP ledger |\n\n---\n\n## 9. Analysis\n\n- **Per mode:** resolved count out of 10, and the median of peak context, total prompt tokens, model calls and wall time.\n- **Per task (paired):** the same task in both modes, side by side in `results.md`, so a difference can be traced to what the agent did (tools used, tiers served, escalations).\n- **Was ACC-MCP used at all?** The number of acc runs in which the model actually called an ACC-MCP tool. If a 4B model ignores the tools, the acc runs measure Pi alone, and that is itself a result.\n- With 10 tasks and one run each, a difference of one or two resolved tasks is within noise. To see the spread, repeat the whole run with a new `--run-id` and report each run, not only the best.\n- Results are reported as they come out, including if ACC-MCP makes things worse.\n\n---\n\n## 10. Threats to validity\n\n- **Small sample:** 10 tasks, one run per task and mode by default.\n- **Injected bugs:** single-line changes are easier to localize than real bugs and may not represent real maintenance work. The reports were written by the project author.\n- **Training data:** both libraries are popular and likely in the model's training data, so the model may recognize the code. This affects both modes equally but can inflate the success rate.\n- **Sampling:** the model's sampling is not seeded; reruns differ.\n- **Hint confound:** acc mode adds one instruction sentence; `--no-hint` runs separate its effect from the tools'.\n- **Token accounting:** context numbers are what llama-server reports to Pi. `maxsplit=1` never stops |\n| `mi_numeric_range_index` | more-itertools | `more.py` (2476) | `numeric_range.index` | `self._start >= value > self._stop` → `self._start > value > self._stop` | `NumericRangeTests` | `.index()` of the first item of a decreasing range raises `ValueError` |\n| `mi_difference` | more-itertools | `more.py` (2940) | `difference` | `map(func, b, a)` → `map(func, a, b)` | `DifferenceTest` | differences come out negated / wrong for custom functions |\n| `mi_is_sorted` | more-itertools | `more.py` (4079) | `is_sorted` | strict and non-strict checks swapped | `IsSortedTests` | `is_sorted([1, 2, 2])` is `False`, with `strict=True` it is `True` |\n| `mi_constrained_batches` | more-itertools | `more.py` (4981) | `constrained_batches` | `> max_size` → `>= max_size` | `ConstrainedBatchesTests` | items that exactly fill `max_size` are split into two batches |\n| `ck_nargs_tuple` | click | `parser.py` (90) | `_unpack_args` | `if spos is not None:` → `if spos is None:` before `x.reverse()` | `test_arguments.py::test_nargs_tup` | `nargs=2` arguments arrive reversed |\n| `ck_int_range_min` | click | `types.py` (664) | `_NumberRangeBase.convert` | `operator.le if self.min_open else operator.lt` → the two operators swapped | `test_types.py::test_range` | `IntRange(5)` rejects `5`; `min_open=True` accepts the bound |\n| `ck_eager_order` | click | `core.py` (164) | `iter_params_for_processing` | `return not item.is_eager, idx` → `return item.is_eager, idx` | `test_commands.py::test_iter_params_for_processing` | eager options (`--version`, `--help`) run after normal ones |\n| `ck_envvar_nargs` | click | `core.py` (2725) | `Parameter.value_from_envvar` | `self.nargs != 1` → `self.nargs > 1` | `test_arguments.py::test_nargs_envvar` | a `nargs=-1` argument no longer splits its environment variable |\n| `ck_help_columns` | click | `formatting.py` (255) | `HelpFormatter.write_dl` | `term_len(first) <= ...` → `term_len(first) < ...` | `test_formatting.py` | in `--help`, the longest option's description wraps to the next line |\n\nExact before/after strings and full bug reports are in `tasks.json`. more-itertools test classes are in `tests/test_more.py`.\n\n### 4.3 Validation (before any run)\n\n`python3 eval/pi_bench.py validate`:\n1. Runs each repository's full test suite on the clean code and stores the failing tests, if any, as the **baseline** (`eval/work/baseline/<repo>.json`). These are not counted against the agent later.\n2. For each task, checks that the \"before\" string occurs exactly once in the file, that the target tests pass on the clean code, and that at least one target test fails with the bug.\n\nA task that fails validation is fixed or dropped before running the benchmark.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Conditions\n\nEach task runs once in each of two modes. The **only** differences between the modes are the ACC-MCP server and one hint sentence.\n\n### 5.1 Held constant in both modes\n\n| Item | Value |\n| :--- | :--- |\n| Model | Qwen3.5-4B GGUF served by `llama-server` at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. The exact file is printed by `doctor` and must be recorded with the results. |\n| Context window | per-slot `n_ctx` read from `llama-server /props` (30,208 on the reference machine), given to Pi as the model's `contextWindow` |\n| Max output per call | 4,096 tokens |\n| Agent | Pi coding agent, non-interactive: `pi --print --mode json --offline` |\n| Tools | Pi's defaults: `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write` |\n| Pi configuration | a fresh `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` per run containing only `models.json`, `settings.json` (and `mcp.json` in acc mode). The user's own MCP servers, skills, prompt templates, themes and `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` files are not loaded (`--no-context-files --no-skills --no-prompt-templates --no-themes`). |\n| Compaction | on, `reserveTokens` 4,096, `keepRecentTokens` 8,000 (Pi's default reserve of 16,384 would leave little of a 30K window) |\n| Prompt | the same template for every task: the bug report, \"find the cause in the library source code and fix it, do not modify or add tests, you can run the tests with `python -m pytest <path>`, reply with one sentence\" |\n| Workspace | a fresh copy of the pinned repo with the bug committed as its only commit |\n| Python for the agent's commands | `eval/work/venv` (Python 3.12 + pytest), first on `PATH`; `PYTHONPATH=src` for click |\n| Time limit | 30 minutes per run; the whole process group is killed after that |\n| Order | for each task, plain then acc, so slow drift (heat, other load) affects both modes alike |\n\n### 5.2 The treatment (acc mode only)\n\n- ACC-MCP is started by Pi as a stdio MCP server (`.venv/bin/python -m acc_mcp.server`) with `direct` exposure, so its tools are declared to the model like built-in tools: `mcp__acc_mcp__get_adaptive_context`, `mcp__acc_mcp__find_symbol`, `mcp__acc_mcp__get_token_ledger`, `mcp__acc_mcp__reset_session`.\n- `ACC_MCP_ROOT` = the task workspace; `ACC_MCP_LEDGER` = a per-run file outside the workspace; session budget 6,000 tokens.\n- One sentence is appended to the system prompt (`ACC_HINT` in `pi_bench.py`): prefer `find_symbol` and `get_adaptive_context` over reading whole files, and call again with `min_tier=3` if a slice is not enough.\n- The built-in tools stay available, so the agent can always fall back to `read` and `bash`.\n\n`--no-hint` runs acc mode without the sentence, to separate the effect of the tools from the effect of the instruction.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Procedure for one run\n\n1. Copy the pinned repo into `eval/work/runs/<run-id>/<mode>/<task>/workspace/` without `.git`, apply the injected change, `git init`, commit everything as \"Initial commit\". Test caches are excluded from git via `.git/info/exclude`.\n2. Write the isolated Pi configuration for the mode (section 5).\n3. Run Pi in the workspace with the task prompt; save its JSON event stream (`events.jsonl`), its session, and stderr.\n4. When Pi exits or times out, save the agent's code changes (`patch.diff`, tests excluded) and record whether it modified anything under `tests/`.\n5. Restore `tests/` to the original, so editing tests cannot make a task pass.\n6. Run the target tests and the full test suite with JUnit reports.\n7. Compute metrics from the events and, in acc mode, from the ACC-MCP ledger.\n8. Write everything to `result.json` and delete the workspace (keep it with `--keep-workspaces`).\n\n---\n\n## 7. Grading\n\nA task is **resolved** when, after step 5:\n- every target test passes (at least one ran), and\n- the full suite has no failing test that was not already failing on the clean repo (the baseline from `validate`).\n\nAlso recorded: whether the agent changed the file that contains the bug, which files it changed, whether it edited tests, and whether the run timed out.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Metrics\n\n| Metric | Definition | Source |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| Resolved | section 7 | test runs |\n| Model calls | number of assistant responses (one per agent step) | `message_end` events |\n| Peak context | largest prompt of a single model call: input + cache-read + cache-write tokens, as llama-server reports them through Pi. Directly comparable to the context window. | `usage` of each assistant message |\n| Total prompt tokens | sum of the prompt sizes over all calls: how much context the model processed for the whole task | same |\n| Output tokens | tokens generated | same |\n| Tool calls / tool output | number of calls and characters returned, per tool | `tool_execution_end` events |\n| Compactions | times Pi had to summarize the conversation to stay in the window | `compaction_start` events |\n| Wall time | seconds from start to exit | runner |\n| ACC-MCP requests, tiers | requests served and their tier (1/2/3), and the tier the decision model picked | ACC-MCP ledger |\n| Escalations | requests where the agent raised `min_tier` above the model's tier | ACC-MCP ledger |\n| Budget step-downs / refusals | slices served one tier lower, or refused, because the session budget was nearly used up | ledger and tool output |\n| ACC-MCP tokens vs whole file | tokens served vs tokens of the whole files those slices came from | ACC-MCP ledger |\n\n---\n\n## 9. Analysis\n\n- **Per mode:** resolved count out of 10, and the median of peak context, total prompt tokens, model calls and wall time.\n- **Per task (paired):** the same task in both modes, side by side in `results.md`, so a difference can be traced to what the agent did (tools used, tiers served, escalations).\n- **Was ACC-MCP used at all?** The number of acc runs in which the model actually called an ACC-MCP tool. If a 4B model ignores the tools, the acc runs measure Pi alone, and that is itself a result.\n- With 10 tasks and one run each, a difference of one or two resolved tasks is within noise. To see the spread, repeat the whole run with a new `--run-id` and report each run, not only the best.\n- Results are reported as they come out, including if ACC-MCP makes things worse.\n\n---\n\n## 10. Threats to validity\n\n- **Small sample:** 10 tasks, one run per task and mode by default.\n- **Injected bugs:** single-line changes are easier to localize than real bugs and may not represent real maintenance work. The reports were written by the project author.\n- **Training data:** both libraries are popular and likely in the model's training data, so the model may recognize the code. This affects both modes equally but can inflate the success rate.\n- **Sampling:** the model's sampling is not seeded; reruns differ.\n- **Hint confound:** acc mode adds one instruction sentence; `--no-hint` runs separate its effect from the tools'.\n- **Token accounting:** context numbers are what llama-server reports to Pi. ACC-MCP's own counts use a different tokenizer (tiktoken or a character estimate), so its tokens and Pi's are compared only within their own source.\n- **One machine, one model:** results hold for this model file, quantization and context size.\n\n---\n\n## 11. Running it\n\nFrom the repository root, with the model already running on port 8080:\n\n```bash\nuv sync                                   # ACC-MCP must be importable from .venv\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py setup            # clone both repos at their tags, create eval/work/venv\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py validate         # baseline + all 10 tasks must be OK\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py doctor           # model, Pi version; acc-mcp must be connected with 4 tools\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py run --tasks mi_difference      # smoke test: one task, both modes\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py run              # all 10 tasks, both modes\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py report           # writes eval/results.md\npython3 eval/pi_bench.py run --mode acc --no-hint --run-id nohint-1   # optional: tools without the hint\n```\n\nOutputs per run are in `eval/work/runs/<run-id>/<mode>/<task>/`: `events.jsonl` (Pi events), `sessions/` (Pi session), `acc_ledger.json`, `patch.diff`, `junit_target.xml`, `junit_full.xml`, `pi_stderr.log`, `result.json`.\n","structuredPatch":[{"oldStart":1,"oldLines":93,"newStart":1,"newLines":197,"lines":[" # Pi Benchmark Protocol (Block 9)"," ","-Does ACC-MCP help a small local model fix bugs in real code, and how much context does it use?
